Optima Academy Online · Teacher Module

Start Here: Set Your Weights and Pacing

M/J World History: Dawn of Civilization to Roman Empire · Florida course 2109010 · Grade 6 · Quarters 3 and 4 (Weeks 19 to 36)
Read this before the quarter starts. Four things in this module are deliberately left for you: the assignment group weights, what you do with the weekly Discussion topics, whether you assign the optional review, and how you describe grading to families. It takes about ten minutes.
Step one

1Set your grade weights in Canvas

The course ships with five weighted assignment groups. Confirm these or change them before the quarter starts. In Canvas go to Assignments, open the ⋮ menu at the top right, and choose Assignment Group Weight.

Assignment groupGroup IDDefault weightWhat lives here
Tier 1: Reading Quizzes72921%All 36 Reading Quizzes (Monday and Wednesday), auto-graded, 5 points each.
Tier 2: Weekly Discussions and Course Reflection73015%Reserved for the weekly Discussions. None are built yet, so this group is empty (see Step 3).
Tier 3: Deep Feedback73134%All 36 Critical Questions and Primary Source Exercises (18 of each), 10 points each, scored with a four-criterion rubric.
Tier 4: Module Check-Ins (Ungraded)7320%Reserved for ungraded scaffolding. The module intro and reflection surveys carry no points and sit in no group.
Quarterly Exams73330%The Quarter 3 Exam and the Quarter 4 Exam only, 36 points each.

The two Quarterly Exams add up to 72 points and the default weight for their group is 30%. That is a recommendation, not a requirement. If you would rather have the exams count for more or less, change the group weight and leave the exam points alone. [VERIFY] Canvas normally leaves an empty group out of the final grade and scales the remaining weights up to fill the space, so with Tier 2 empty the effective weights are higher than the table shows. Check one student's grade in your gradebook before you tell families a number.

Step two

2Know what is optional

The Optional Cumulative Review is the last item in the Week 36 module. It is a Canvas practice quiz, not an assignment, so it never reaches the gradebook. Students may take it as many times as they like, and the correct answers show when they finish. Assign it, suggest it, or ignore it, as you see fit.

The two Quarterly Exams are not optional. The Quarter 3 Exam is the last item in the Week 27 module and the Quarter 4 Exam is the last item in the Week 36 module. Each covers its own quarter only.

Step three

3Know what is not built yet

This module describes the course as it exists today. These parts are planned but not part of the course yet, so do not look for them:

  • Weekly Discussions. Every week has a planned discussion topic (listed week by week in the manual), but no Discussion is built. Use the topics as live seminar prompts, or set up your own Discussion in Tier 2.
  • VR activities. Every week reserves two platform-neutral VR slots, but no activity is written yet.
  • Interactive widgets, appendices, and some maps. The lessons and primary-source pages are text pages. Lessons in Weeks 28 to 36 carry a geographical glossary but no map image, and the manual lists the two images that may not load.
  • Verified primary-source wording. The excerpts students read in the Critical Questions and the Primary Source Exercises are close adaptations of public-domain translations. They have not yet been checked word for word against the published translations. Treat them as faithful in meaning, not as quotations.

The manual lists every one of these again, with the reason and what comes next.

Step four

4Describe grading to families yourself

This module does not include a syllabus. Use your own section syllabus, and write its grading section to match whatever weights you chose in Step 1. Do not average the numbers in your syllabus with the numbers in the Canvas table above. Set the Canvas weights first, then write the syllabus to describe what you set.

Section

Where to go next

Open the Teacher Manual (Facilitator Copy), the next item in this module. Read Sections 0 to 3 and Section 5 before your first week. Keep Sections 6 to 8 open while you grade, and read Section 15 before the weeks it flags.

This is the facilitator guide for Quarters 3 and 4 of M/J World History: Dawn of Civilization to Roman Empire, Weeks 19 to 36. The first half of the course (Weeks 1 to 18) has its own manual. Read Sections 1, 2, 3, and 5 before your first week, keep Sections 6, 7, and 8 open while you grade, use Section 11 to plan pacing and see what each week covers, and read Section 15 before the weeks it flags. Every count, group number, and point value below was read from the live course, not assumed from build notes.

2How this course works: typical lesson, typical module, major assessments

A typical lesson page. Every one of the 36 lessons and 36 primary-source pages is a standalone page hosted on GitHub Pages and embedded in its Canvas page by iframe, never merely linked. Each lesson opens with a Glossary of Subject Vocabulary box, carries a separate Foreign Language Vocabulary box near the first foreign term, and uses hover definitions with a pronunciation for glossed words. Lessons that carry a main map include a geographical glossary; the rest carry the glossary alone. Callouts cover the figures, peoples, technology, battles, and cities of the week. A term is glossed where it first appears in a lesson and may be glossed again in any later lesson.

The graded work is never on the lesson page. It is the separate Canvas items that follow it in the module.

A typical module. One numbered module is one week. Module 19 is Week 19, and so on to Module 36. Every module has the same shape, and items are numbered by their order in the module (for example 24.1, 24.2, 24.9).

3The intro and reflection surveys

Two things new facilitators most often misread:

  • The hover glossary costs you nothing. It gives students a definition and a pronunciation and never produces a submission. A student who skips it shows it indirectly, in a weaker quiz score or a thinner written answer, not as a missing grade. Do not build a gradebook column for it.
  • The surveys are Canvas quizzes in survey mode, not pages. That is what makes the answers sortable across your whole roster.

The single highest-leverage move in the course. Spend 15 to 20 minutes reading each module's reflection answers as a set. Sort for low confidence and for repeated "still unclear" topics, post one targeted announcement on the top confusion, and message the two or three students whose confidence is lowest. This finds struggling students before a grade would.

Section

4VR in this course

Every week reserves two solo VR activity slots, in platform-neutral language (for example, explore, compare, build, trace). None has been written yet. Until they are, use the week's lesson and primary sources as the whole week's work. How VR work will be graded has not been decided, and this manual will say so when it is. Do not add vendor or product names to any VR text in this course. That is deliberate.

Section

Common mix-up. Critical Questions and Primary Source Exercises look like light Tier 2 work at a glance, since each is two short written answers. They are deliberately in Tier 3, because both are graded on the quality of reasoning and have no single right answer. Check the group column, not the item's length, before assuming a tier.

Empty groups. Tier 2 and Tier 4 hold nothing today. [VERIFY] Canvas normally leaves an empty group out of the final grade and scales the remaining weights up. With Tier 2 empty, Tier 1, Tier 3, and the exams share the whole grade, in roughly the ratio 21 : 34 : 30. Look at one student's grade before you quote a percentage to a family.

  1. Gradebook, then Settings, then "Weight final grade based on assignment groups". Confirm the five groups and their weights (21 / 15 / 34 / 0 / 30), or set your own.
  2. Confirm each item sits in the right group: Reading Quizzes in Tier 1, Critical Questions and Primary Source Exercises in Tier 3, the two exams in Quarterly Exams, even though they are auto-graded multiple choice.
  3. Confirm the intro and reflection surveys on every module are surveys with zero points and no assignment group, so they gather information without changing grades.
  4. The recommended default is that the two exams together count for about 30% of the course grade. You may change it. Adjust the group weight and leave the exam points alone.
Section

6Rubrics and answer guides for teacher-graded items

The course carries 36 Canvas rubrics, one per Tier 3 item, all on the same four-criterion base. Each is worth 10 points.

CriterionPoints
Understanding of the material2.5
Quality of reasoning2.5
Clarity and precision of expression2.5
Intellectual honesty (naming the limits of your own understanding)2.5
Total10

Every Critical Questions set has exactly two questions, one per excerpt, and every Primary Source Exercise has exactly two open-ended questions. The questions rotate among counterfactual, causation, and conceptual types, and the type is never named to students.

Answer guides: teacher only. Full credit on a conceptual question means the student names an idea at work in the source that the source never states outright. Example, Week 22, Critical Questions: Demaratus tells Xerxes the Spartans are free, yet law is their master. A full-credit answer says that freedom here means obeying laws the community itself chose and honors, not following a master's whim, and ties this to the phalanx, where each man has to trust the man beside him. A partial answer only restates that the Spartans obey their law. Full credit on a counterfactual question needs an argument, not a guess. Example, Week 29: if Cincinnatus had kept his office for the full six months or longer, a full-credit answer uses the excerpt to say what Romans trusted a dictator to do and what they feared if he did not give up power, with evidence from the lessons. Whatever conclusion the student reaches, judge the reasoning, not the verdict.

The excerpts themselves. The quoted passages are close adaptations written for this course (see Section 1). When a student says the wording does not match the book they found, they may be right. Do not mark down a student for quoting a published translation.

Section

8Quarterly exams and the optional review

There are two Quarterly Exams. The Quarter 3 Exam (Canvas quiz 5426, the last item in the Week 27 module) covers Weeks 19 to 27, and the Quarter 4 Exam (quiz 5427, the last item in the Week 36 module) covers Weeks 28 to 36. Each has 36 multiple-choice questions worth 1 point each, with two questions per lesson, and allows one attempt. Neither is cumulative. Correct answers stay hidden after submission so the exam can be reused, and you can change that in the quiz settings. Every question has a short explanation in the answer key. The questions are new and none repeats a Reading Quiz question. Grade 6 World History has no End-of-Course exam, so the exams aim for fair coverage of the quarter, not for any state test.

Both exams sit in their own Quarterly Exams group (id 733). That is a deliberate choice, recorded in Section 13.

The optional Cumulative Review (quiz 5430, the last item in the Week 36 module) is a 40-question practice quiz covering Weeks 19 to 36 in course order. 6 of its questions tie two lessons together, for example Greek hoplites and Roman citizen-soldiers, or the way Rome treated its allies compared with the way Athens treated the members of its league. It has unlimited attempts and is not attached to any assignment, so it never touches the gradebook.

Section

9Teacher workflow and workload map

A normal week, in order: read the previous module's reflection answers and post one announcement, then batch-grade the week's Critical Questions and Primary Source Exercise, then answer messages. Tier 1 grades itself at near zero teacher time, and the two exams grade themselves twice a year.

The Tier 3 load is high, and that is an accepted cost, not a build error. The general guidance for Optima courses is that deep, teacher-graded work should be roughly 10 to 15% of graded items. Here, 36 of the 74 graded items (about 49%) are in Tier 3, because every week carries two written-response items, a Critical Questions set and a Primary Source Exercise, rather than one. The course lead accepted that cost in the first half of the course and it carries over. Do not re-propose splitting them.

12Vocabulary and reading-level conventions

Lessons are written at a sixth-grade reading level for the prose, with a target of about 1,000 words (floor 800, ceiling 1,200). Subject terms and foreign terms, including the names of figures with Greek or Latin forms, are glossed and may read above grade level on purpose, because a student cannot learn the subject without them.

Measured, by quarter. The 18 lessons of Quarter 3 run 802 to 1001 words, at a measured Flesch-Kincaid grade level of 4.3 to 6.1 for the prose. The 18 lessons of Quarter 4 run 800 to 900 words, at 4.1 to 6. These counts leave out the glossary boxes and callouts, and the grade level is a rough guide, since proper names and glossed terms are excluded from the target. Do not represent the lessons to a family as a fixed grade level beyond that.

Glossing. The Glossary of Subject Vocabulary sits at the very top of a lesson, in alphabetical order, each entry with a short definition and a phonetic spelling. A separate Foreign Language Vocabulary box sits further down, near the first foreign term, with the English gloss in bold and the foreign term in italics. A term is glossed where it first appears within a lesson. It may be glossed again in a later lesson, but within one lesson only its first appearance is marked.

Dates. All dates are given as BC, never BCE.

13Documented, accepted exceptions

These are deliberate decisions, made and recorded by the course lead. Do not "fix" any of them without revisiting the decision first.

  • Tier 3 carries about 49% of graded items. Every week has two written-response items, and both are placed in Tier 3 rather than splitting one into a lighter tier. Accepted; do not re-propose splitting them.
  • The Quarterly Exams sit in their own assignment group (30%), not inside Tier 1 or Tier 3. A dedicated group makes the intended weight exact. The cost is a fifth top-level category.
  • The review is optional and never graded. Middle school reports quarter and course grades and does not require a cumulative exam. The review is a practice quiz so that it cannot reach the gradebook.
  • Primary-source excerpts are adaptations. They were written for this course from public-domain translations and are being checked against them. They are flagged here and in the build log so that no one passes them off as verbatim.
  • Not all lessons carry a map image. Weeks 28 to 36 carry a geographical glossary alone, and two image links (Lessons 19.1 and 27.2) may fail to load. Map and image work is scheduled for the wrap-up pass.
  • The M365 digital-skills surface is not part of this half of the course. It was left out on purpose for now.

14What makes this course classical

  • Contingency first. Every week turns on at least one moment where history could have gone another way: the Spartan expulsion of a tyrant in 510 BC, Marathon, Salamis, Hannibal after Cannae, the Rubicon, the Ides of March, and Alexander's early death. The counterfactual questions in the Critical Questions rotation exist for this.
  • Great Men and Great Events as the narrative spine. Solon, Cleisthenes, Pericles, Alexander, Hannibal, Scipio, Caesar, Augustus, and Constantine are named and judged directly, not routed to a sidebar.
  • Classical Republican evaluation. Regimes are judged by whether their laws, customs, and habits solve the first-order problems of a city: who rules, who counts as a citizen, who fights, and how power is kept in check. Sparta, Athens, the Roman Republic, and the principate are compared on those terms.
  • Primary sources every week. Students meet Hesiod, Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, Polybius, Livy, Caesar, and Pliny directly in short excerpts, not only a summary of them.
  • No tidy story of progress. The collapse of the Republic and the crisis of the third century are presented as results of choices and accidents, with the causes still argued over.

assignments.title: 19.1 Critical Questions: Hesiod, Works and Days
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

So there was never just one kind of Strife. There are two on the earth. One a man would praise when he understood her, and the other he would blame, for they have quite different hearts. One makes ugly war and fighting grow. She is cruel, and no man loves her, but men honor this heavy Strife because the gods require it.

The other is the elder daughter of dark Night. She stirs even the helpless man to work. A man grows eager for work when he looks at his neighbor, a rich man who hurries to plant and sow and put his house in good order. Neighbor competes with neighbor as he hurries after wealth. This Strife is good for men.

Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 11 to 24 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Hesiod says there are two kinds of Strife, which is the Greek idea of contest. Using what you learned in Lesson 19.1, explain how Hesiod's good Strife differs from the contest Homer's heroes pursued, and why a city might want one kind and fear the other.

Excerpt 2

But those who give straight judgments to strangers and to their own people, and never turn aside from what is just, their city blooms, and the people in it flourish. Famine never keeps company with men who judge straight.

But for those who practice violence and cruel deeds, Zeus, who sees from far away, appoints a punishment. Often even a whole city suffers because of one bad man.

Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 225 to 231 and 240 to 241 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Imagine that the judges of a Greek polis began taking gifts from rich men and ruling in their favor. Using Hesiod's words and what you know about his quarrel with his brother, explain what Hesiod would expect to happen to that city, and what an ordinary farmer might do. Use what you learned in Lesson 19.1 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 19.2 Primary Source Exercise: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Lycurgus made a rule that only iron money should be used. He gave it a small value for its great weight, so that a sum of ten minas needed a large storeroom in the house and a yoke of oxen to carry it.

When this money became the custom, many kinds of wrongdoing left Sparta. For who would steal it, or take it as a bribe, or rob for it, when it could not be hidden, could not be enjoyed, and could not even be cut up to any profit?

Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, chapter 9 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch wrote many hundreds of years after the time of Lycurgus.

Question 1. Plutarch says iron money reduced wrongdoing in Sparta. Explain the reasoning behind his claim. Then use Lesson 19.2 to describe one other effect that iron money may have had on Sparta, even though Plutarch does not mention it here.

Question 2. Plutarch admits that no one agrees when Lycurgus lived, and he wrote long after. Choose one thing in this passage that you think we can reasonably trust and one thing we should question. Explain your thinking for each, and say what else you would want to know. Use what you learned in Lesson 19.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 20.1 Critical Questions: Aristotle on Solon
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Three of Solon's measures seem the most democratic. First and most important, he banned loans that were secured on a man's own person. Second, he allowed anyone who wished to seek justice on behalf of people who were wronged. Third, he gave the right of appeal to the jury-courts. They say this is what chiefly gave strength to the people, for when the people are master of the vote, they are master of the state.

Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians, chapter 9 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Aristotle says the right of appeal to the jury-courts gave the people their chief strength. Explain why that right could matter so much to the thetes, who could hold no office, and what Aristotle means when he says that whoever controls the vote controls the state. Use what you learned in Lesson 20.1 to support your answer.

Excerpt 2

I gave the common people as much honor as is enough, taking nothing from their dignity and reaching for nothing more. As for those who had power and were admired for their wealth, I took care that they too should suffer no insult. I stood with a strong shield in front of both, and I let neither side win unjustly.

Solon, quoted in Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians, chapter 12 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Imagine that Solon had given the poor what they asked for and divided the land of the rich. Using this poem and Lesson 20.1, explain what you think might have happened to Athens, and why.

assignments.title: 20.2 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus on the Athenians Freed
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

So the Athenians grew in power. And it is clear, not from one example but in every way, that equality of speech is a good thing. While the Athenians were ruled by tyrants they were no better in war than any of their neighbors, but once they were rid of the tyrants they became by far the first.

This shows that when they were held down they fought below their strength, as men working for a master. But when they were freed, each man was eager to work for himself.

Herodotus, Histories, book 5, chapter 78 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Herodotus gives one explanation for why Athens grew strong after the tyrants. State it in your own words. Then use Lesson 20.2 to explain which changes made by Cleisthenes could have produced the eagerness Herodotus describes.

Question 2. Herodotus praises equality of speech, yet Lesson 20.2 reminds us that women, slaves, and foreigners living in Athens had no voice in the Assembly. Explain how both things can be true. Does the second fact weaken what Herodotus claims? Give your reasons.

assignments.title: 21.1 Critical Questions: Herodotus on Sardis
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

It seems that it is easier to deceive a crowd than one man. Aristagoras could not deceive Cleomenes of Sparta, who was alone, but he deceived thirty thousand Athenians. The Athenians voted to send twenty ships to help the Ionians. These ships were the beginning of evils for Greeks and for foreigners.

Herodotus, Histories, book 5, chapter 97 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Herodotus blames the Athenian vote on a crowd being deceived. What does this suggest about how he viewed a large assembly? What might a defender of the Athenian Assembly say in reply, using what you know from Lessons 20.2 and 21.1?

Excerpt 2

When Darius heard of the burning of Sardis, he asked who the Athenians were. When he was told, he asked for his bow. He set an arrow on it and shot it up toward the sky, and as it flew he said, "Zeus, grant that I may punish the Athenians."

Then he ordered one of his servants to say to him three times whenever his dinner was served, "Master, remember the Athenians."

Herodotus, Histories, book 5, chapter 105 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Suppose Athens had never sent the twenty ships to Ionia. Using this passage and Lesson 21.1, explain whether you think a Persian army would still have landed at Marathon in 490 BC, and what makes you more or less sure.

assignments.title: 21.2 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus on Marathon
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Miltiades spoke to Callimachus: "With you now, Callimachus, it rests either to enslave Athens or to make her free, and so to leave behind for all time a memorial such as not even Harmodius and Aristogeiton left. For now Athens is in the greatest danger she has ever known. If she bows to the Medes, her fate is settled, for she will be handed over to Hippias. But if our city wins, she may become the first city of Greece."

The Athenians charged the foreigners at a run. They were the first Greeks we know of to charge at a run, and the first to bear the sight of Median dress and of men wearing it. Until then the very name of the Medes was a terror to the Greeks.

Herodotus, Histories, book 6, chapters 109 and 112 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Herodotus could not have heard the speech of Miltiades. Explain what a historian should do with a speech like this. Then explain how it connects to the idea in Lesson 21.2 that one vote may have decided the fate of Athens.

Question 2. Herodotus says the Athenians were the first to charge at a run and the first to endure the sight of Median dress. Explain what this suggests about the part played by fear and confidence in the battle, and whether you think this mattered more than the Greek armor and spears. Give your reasons. Use what you learned in Lesson 21.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 22.1 Critical Questions: Herodotus on the Spartans
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Demaratus, an exiled Spartan king, tells Xerxes about the Spartans: "They are free, but not wholly free. Law is their master, and they fear it far more than your men fear you. They do whatever it commands, and its command is always the same: not to flee in battle from any number of men, but to stay in their ranks and win or die."

Herodotus, Histories, book 7, chapter 104 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Demaratus says the Spartans are free, yet law is their master. Explain how a person can be both. Use what you learned in Lessons 19.1 and 22.1 about the phalanx to say why this kind of obedience might make an army stronger.

Excerpt 2

Before the fighting, a man from Trachis told the Spartan Dienekes that the Persian arrows were so many that when they shot, they hid the sun. Dienekes was not afraid. He made light of the number of the Medes and said, "Our Trachinian guest brings us good news. If the Medes hide the sun, we shall have our fight in the shade."

Herodotus, Histories, book 7, chapter 226 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Herodotus was not at Thermopylae and wrote about forty years later. Explain what this story shows about how the Spartans were taught to meet fear, and what its being a story told afterward means for how far we should trust it. Use what you learned in Lesson 22.1 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 22.2 Primary Source Exercise: Aeschylus, The Persians
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

The Persian queen asks about the Athenians: "Who is the master set over their army?" The chorus answers: "They are called the slaves of no man, nor the subjects of any."

A messenger describes the Greek battle cry at Salamis: "Come, sons of the Greeks! Free your fatherland, free your children and your wives, the temples of your fathers' gods, and the tombs of your ancestors. Now the fight is for all."

Aeschylus, The Persians, lines 241 to 242 and 402 to 405 (adapted from a public-domain translation). The play was first performed in Athens in 472 BC, eight years after Salamis.

Question 1. The play was written for an Athenian audience, yet these lines are spoken by Persians and about Persians. Explain what this choice suggests about how Aeschylus and his audience pictured the war. Why might showing the war from the other side make the Greek victory seem more meaningful? Use what you learned in Lesson 22.2 to support your answer.

Question 2. The battle cry says "the fight is for all." Lesson 22.2 says Greek unity was the exception, not the rule. Explain what would have to be true for "all" to be an accurate word, and point to a place where it strains.

assignments.title: 23.1 Critical Questions: Thucydides, The Funeral Oration
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Our form of government does not copy the laws of our neighbors. We are an example to others more than imitators of them. It is called a democracy, because power is in the hands of the many and not of the few. The law gives equal justice to all in their private disputes, yet the claim of excellence is also honored. When a citizen is distinguished in any way, he is preferred for public service, not as a privilege, but as the reward of merit. Nor does poverty stand in the way.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 2, chapter 37 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Pericles says Athens is ruled by the many yet rewards merit. Do these two claims fit together, or do they pull against each other? Use what you learned in Lesson 23.1 about the lot, the juries, and pay for service to support your answer.

Excerpt 2

We alone regard a man who takes no part in public affairs not as harmless, but as a useless character.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 2, chapter 40 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Suppose Athens had stopped paying citizens for jury service. Using this sentence and Lesson 23.1, explain who might have stopped taking part and how that could change what Pericles is boasting about.

assignments.title: 23.2 Primary Source Exercise: Sophocles, Antigone
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Creon, the king, declares: "Whoever thinks a friend more important than his own country, I count him as nothing."

Antigone answers him: "I did not think your decrees had such power that you, a mortal, could override the unwritten and unshakable laws of the gods. They are not of today or yesterday, but live always, and no one knows from where they came."

Sophocles, Antigone, lines 182 to 183 and 450 to 457 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. State in your own words what Creon puts first and what Antigone puts first. Then explain which of their claims you find stronger in the situation of the play, and what each would say is the greatest danger to a city. Use what you learned in Lesson 23.2 to support your answer.

Question 2. Thousands of Athenian citizens watched this play, and many also served on juries and voted in the Assembly. Imagine you are one of them. Explain how having seen the play might change how you judge a person who broke a law for a reason of conscience. Give your reasoning, not just your conclusion. Use what you learned in Lesson 23.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 24.1 Critical Questions: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

As for the reasons each side gave for breaking the peace, I have written them down, so that no one need ask how so great a war came upon the Greeks. But the truest cause, though the one least spoken of, I believe to be this. The Athenians were growing great, and this frightened the Spartans and forced them into war.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 1, chapter 23 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Suppose Corcyra, Potidaea, and Megara had never quarreled with anyone. Using this passage and Lesson 24.1, explain whether Thucydides would expect the war to have been avoided. What does your answer show about the difference between the spark that starts a war and the cause beneath it?

Excerpt 2

No fear of the gods or law of men held anyone back. As to the gods, people judged it was the same whether they worshiped or not, since they saw everyone dying alike. As to the law, no one expected to live long enough to be brought to trial and pay for his crimes. Each thought that a far heavier sentence was already hanging over him, and that before it fell he might as well enjoy something of life.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 2, chapter 53 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Thucydides says the plague harmed Athens in another way besides sickness. Explain what he says broke down in the city, and why a city might depend on that even more than on good doctors. Use what you learned in Lesson 24.1 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 24.2 Primary Source Exercise: Thucydides, The Melian Dialogue
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

The Athenians say: "You know as well as we do that, in the world as it is, right is only a question between equals in power. The strong do what they can, and the weak accept what they must."

The Melians answer: "We trust that the gods will give us as good fortune as you, because we stand for what is right against what is wrong. And what we lack, we trust that the Spartans will supply."

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 5, chapters 89 and 104 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Thucydides says he gives the speeches as he thought the speakers would have spoken.

Question 1. State the Athenian argument and the Melian answer in your own words. Then explain what each side expected would happen next, and use Lesson 24.2 to tell what actually happened. Which expectation turned out to be closer to the truth, and why?

Question 2. Thucydides tells us he wrote these speeches as he thought the speakers would have spoken. How does that affect how far we can trust this passage as a record of what was really said? What can it still tell us about Athens and about Thucydides himself? Use what you learned in Lesson 24.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 25.1 Critical Questions: Plato, Apology of Socrates
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

I went to one of those who seemed wise. When I examined him, I found that he seemed wise to many people and above all to himself, but he was not. I tried to show him that he thought he was wise and was not, and so I became hated by him and by many who were there.

I thought to myself: I am wiser than this man. Neither of us knows anything fine and good, but he thinks he knows something when he does not, while I, since I do not know, do not think I know. In this small matter I seem to be wiser, that what I do not know I do not think I know.

Plato, Apology of Socrates, around sections 21 to 23 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Socrates says he is wiser only because he does not think he knows what he does not know. Using Lesson 25.1, explain why the men he questioned might have been angry with him instead of thankful, and what that anger might have meant for Socrates years later.

Excerpt 2

Men of Athens, I honor and love you, but I will obey the god rather than you. As long as I breathe and am able, I will not stop practicing philosophy, urging and showing anyone I meet that he should care for the best state of his soul more than for money or reputation.

Plato, Apology of Socrates, around sections 29 and 30 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Socrates tells the jury he will not stop asking questions even if they order him to. Using Lesson 25.1, explain how this promise might have affected the vote of the jury. Then name one other factor from the lesson, apart from anything he said, that might also have mattered.

assignments.title: 25.2 Primary Source Exercise: Xenophon, Hellenica
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Almost everyone had supposed that if so great a battle were fought, those who won would rule and those who lost would obey. But the god so ordered it that each side set up a trophy as though it had won, and neither tried to stop the other from doing so. Each gave back the dead under truce as if beaten, and each took up its own dead as if victorious. Each claimed the victory, yet neither was seen to be any better off in land, in city, or in power than before the battle. There was even more confusion and uncertainty in Greece after it than before.

Xenophon, Hellenica, book 7, near the end of chapter 5 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Xenophon says people expected the winners of the great battle to rule and the others to obey. Explain, using what Lesson 25.2 says about Thebes and the other cities, why that did not happen.

Question 2. Xenophon admired Sparta, had known Socrates, and wrote about events he lived through. Choose one claim in this passage that you think we can reasonably trust and one that we should handle with care. Explain your reasoning for each. Use what you learned in Lesson 25.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 26.1 Critical Questions: Demosthenes, First Philippic
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

No one should suppose that Philip can be stopped by hired soldiers alone. Men who fight for pay will serve whoever pays them. Let part of our force be our own citizens, so that the army belongs to us and has something of its own to defend.

Demosthenes, First Philippic (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Suppose the Athenians had taken this advice and every citizen had served in the army. Using Lesson 26.1, explain one way this might have changed Athens's answer to Philip, and one reason many Athenians might still have refused to do it.

Excerpt 2

You Athenians behave like a barbarian boxer. When he is struck in one place, his hands go there. If he is hit somewhere else, his hands go there. He neither knows how to guard against a blow nor tries to look ahead. In the same way, if you hear that Philip is in one place, you vote to send help there. If he turns up elsewhere, you hurry after him. You never plan ahead.

Demosthenes, First Philippic (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Demosthenes compares the Athenians to a boxer who only guards where he was last hit. In your own words, explain what he thinks the Athenians are doing wrong, and use Lesson 26.1 to describe a habit that would have been a better answer to Philip.

assignments.title: 26.2 Primary Source Exercise: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Parmenion, the older general, advised Alexander to attack the Persians by night. Their numbers were so great, he said, that the darkness would hide how few the Macedonians were, and the sudden attack would throw them into confusion. Alexander is said to have answered that he would not steal a victory. He wanted Darius to have no excuse for being beaten, and no way to blame the darkness or a surprise for his defeat.

Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, book 3, chapter 10 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander.

Question 1. Explain the reasoning of Parmenion and the answer Alexander is said to give. What does Alexander seem to value more than a safe win, and what might he have risked by choosing it? Use what you learned in Lesson 26.2 to support your answer.

Question 2. Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander, and he says only that the king is said to have answered this way. Explain how far you would trust this exchange as a true record of what was said, and what the story could still tell us even if the words are not exact. Use what you learned in Lesson 26.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 27.1 Critical Questions: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Coenus spoke for the soldiers. "Sire, a ruler must know when to stop. You see how few of the Macedonians and Greeks who set out with you are left. Some were sent home, some died, and some, worn out or wounded, were left behind in the cities. Those of us who remain have no strength for more. All of us long to see our parents, wives, and children again. Go home, sire, and then, if you wish, lead another army."

Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, book 5, chapter 27 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander.

Question 1. Using Lesson 27.1, explain why the request of the soldiers was so powerful, and what it shows about what even a great king depends on.

Excerpt 2

Callisthenes spoke against the bowing. "Alexander, I think you worthy of every honor that a man can have. But honors for men and honors for gods have always been kept apart. Among the Greeks, no one bows down to a man. You came to add Asia to Greece, and you rule Greeks, so remember Greece."

Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, book 4, chapter 11 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander.

Question 2. Suppose Alexander had insisted that every Macedonian and Greek bow to him in the Persian way. Using this excerpt and Lesson 27.1, explain what a Persian and a Macedonian would each have thought the bow meant, and what risk Alexander ran by demanding it.

assignments.title: 27.2 Primary Source Exercise: Asoka, Thirteenth Rock Edict
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

When he had been king for eight years, the Beloved of the Gods conquered Kalinga. A hundred and fifty thousand people were carried away, a hundred thousand were killed, and many times that number died. After that, the Beloved of the Gods felt deep sorrow for having conquered Kalinga, for when a land is conquered, the killing and the carrying away of people weigh heavily on him. He now holds that the best conquest is the conquest by Dhamma, which means right living. This conquest has been won here, and also in the lands on the borders, even where the Greek king Antiochus rules.

Asoka, Thirteenth Rock Edict (adapted from a public-domain translation). The king speaks of himself as the Beloved of the Gods.

Question 1. Asoka says he felt deep sorrow after the conquest of Kalinga and now values conquest by Dhamma more than conquest by war. Explain his reasoning. Then compare it with how Lessons 26.2 and 27.1 show Alexander treating Thebes and Tyre. What does the comparison show about what different rulers thought a conqueror owes to people?

Question 2. This text was carved in stone by order of the king himself, and some of his edicts were also written in Greek. Explain what a king might want his people to believe when he carves such a statement, and what that means for how much we can trust it. What can the passage still tell us, for example about the reach of Greek power and the Greek language? Use what you learned in Lesson 27.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 28.1 Critical Questions: Livy, History of Rome
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

The beginning of freedom should be dated from the fact that the power of the consuls was made yearly, and not from any lessening of the power the kings had held. The first consuls kept all the rights and signs of rule that the kings had had.

Livy, History of Rome, book 2, chapter 1 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Livy says freedom began because the consuls' power lasted only a year, not because it was made smaller. Using Lesson 28.1, explain why a limit on time might protect Romans from a king as well as a limit on power would have, and what dangers might still remain.

Excerpt 2

Once, when the parts of the human body did not all agree as they do now, the other parts grew angry that all their care and labor went to feed the belly, while the belly sat idle in the middle and enjoyed what they brought. They agreed that the hands should carry no food to the mouth, nor the mouth take it, nor the teeth chew it. But while they tried to starve the belly into obeying, the limbs and the whole body wasted away. Then they saw that the belly's work was not idle. It was fed, and it fed them in turn, sending back to every part the blood by which we live.

Livy, History of Rome, book 2, chapter 32 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Livy says this story was told to plebeians who had marched out of Rome. In your own words, explain what the speaker wants them to think about patricians and plebeians. Then use Lesson 28.1 to give one reason the plebeians might not have been fully satisfied by the story alone.

assignments.title: 28.2 Primary Source Exercise: Polybius, The Roman Constitution
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

If we look at the power of the consuls, the government seems entirely kingly. If we look at the Senate, it seems an aristocracy. And if we look at the power of the people, it seems plainly a democracy.

Each of these three parts can either hinder or help the others. None of them can act alone, and none can work against the rest without being checked. So the government is well fitted to meet every emergency, and it is hard to find a better one.

Polybius, Histories, book 6, chapters 11 and 18 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius was a Greek who lived in Rome as a young man.

Question 1. Explain in your own words how Polybius says the three parts of the Roman government depend on one another. Then use Lesson 28.2 to give one example of a check that one part had on another, and say whether it matches his description.

Question 2. Polybius was a Greek who had been taken to Rome and who admired what he saw. Name one way this might make him a good observer and one way it might lead him to miss or to overlook something. Use Lesson 28.2, for example what it says about who counted as a citizen, to support your answer.

assignments.title: 29.1 Critical Questions: Livy, History of Rome
assignments.html:
