Excerpt 1

He was found plowing his land. After greetings were exchanged, the messengers said, "May the gods bless you and your country. The Senate asks that you put on your toga and hear its orders." Astonished, he asked, "Is all well?" and told his wife to bring his toga from the hut. He wiped the dust and sweat from himself, put it on, and came forward. Then the messengers hailed him as dictator.

Livy, History of Rome, book 3, chapter 26 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Livy takes care to show Cincinnatus at work on his own land when the Senate calls him. Using Lesson 29.1, explain why Livy and the Romans who loved this story might have wanted readers to picture him this way.

Excerpt 2

The dictator, who had been named for six months, laid down his office on the sixteenth day, having ended the war and saved the army.

Livy, History of Rome, book 3, chapter 29 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Suppose Cincinnatus had kept his office for the full six months, or longer. Using this excerpt and Lessons 28.2 and 29.1, explain what the Romans trusted a dictator to do, and what a Roman might have feared if he had not given up power.

assignments.title: 29.2 Primary Source Exercise: Polybius, The Romans Build a Navy
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

It was at this time that the Romans first thought seriously of the sea. They had no ships and no skill at rowing, yet they dared to try. They began with such boldness that before they had ever tried the sea they challenged the Carthaginians, who had held command of it for generations.

A ship of the Carthaginians had run aground, and the Romans used it as a model. They built a hundred large ships, and while the ships were being built they seated the crews on rowing benches on dry land and taught them to row by drill.

Polybius, Histories, book 1, chapters 20 and 21 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius was a Greek who wrote about the rise of Rome.

Question 1. Polybius says the Romans challenged Carthage at sea before they had ever tried the sea. Use this passage and Lesson 29.2 to explain what this shows about Roman boldness, and what weakness the corvus was meant to make up for.

Question 2. Polybius was a Greek who admired Rome, yet Lesson 29.2 says he thought it was unjust for Rome to seize Sardinia and Corsica. Explain how that fact affects how far you would trust his praise of Roman boldness here, and what a writer who both admires and criticizes a people can tell us.

assignments.title: 30.1 Critical Questions: Polybius, Histories
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Hannibal saw that his soldiers were downcast from the long march and its hardships. He called them together and, having no other encouragement to give, showed them Italy, which lies so close beneath the Alps that, seen together, the mountains seem to be the walls of the whole country. He pointed out the plains of the Po, and reminded them of the friendly feeling of the Gauls who lived there, and he pointed the way to Rome itself. By this he lifted their spirits.

Polybius, Histories, book 3, chapter 54 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. From the top of the Alps, Hannibal points to Italy and to Rome. Using Lesson 30.1, explain what he wants his tired soldiers to feel, and why that mattered so much for an army so far from home.

Excerpt 2

When Hannibal set out from Spain he had about ninety thousand foot soldiers and twelve thousand horsemen. But when he came down into Italy he had in all only about twenty thousand foot soldiers and not more than six thousand horsemen.

Polybius, Histories, book 3, chapters 35 and 56 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius says he took the figures from a record Hannibal himself set up.

Question 2. Compare the two sets of numbers. Using Lesson 30.1, explain what they show about the cost of the march, and why a general who arrives with so many fewer men might have to win by trick and not by size.

assignments.title: 30.2 Primary Source Exercise: Polybius, The Battle of Zama
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Hannibal said to Scipio: "Consider how quickly fortune can change. I myself stand before you as an example. I once fought you in Italy and had your whole country in fear, and now I am here to ask for the lives of my people. You are young and have never been beaten. But a wise man does not trust his good luck at the height of his success."

In that battle Hannibal acted as a skilled and tried general should. He had used every resource before the fight, and he held nothing back. But he was beaten.

Polybius, Histories, book 15, around chapters 6 and 16 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius was a friend of Scipio's family.

Question 1. Hannibal warns Scipio how quickly fortune can change. Explain what he is asking Scipio to do and why he thinks it is wise. Then use Lesson 30.2 to tell what Scipio actually did, and whether the later lives of the two men show that Hannibal's warning applied to Scipio too.

Question 2. Use the passage and Lessons 30.1 and 30.2 to give your own answer to this week's question: was Hannibal a genius, a gambler, or both? Give one piece of evidence on each side. Then say what you would want to check, since a friend of Scipio's family is giving us this judgment.

assignments.title: 31.1 Critical Questions: Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

The wild beasts that roam over Italy have each a den to lie in, but the men who fight and die for Italy have nothing but air and light. Without house or home they wander about with their wives and children. They fight and die to give wealth and comfort to others. They are called the masters of the world, and they have not a clod of earth that is their own.

Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus, chapter 9 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 1. Plutarch gives Tiberius these words about Roman soldiers. Using Lesson 31.1, explain who the soldiers were and what had happened to their farms, and why a speech like this might make rich senators afraid.

Excerpt 2

The rich, by offering higher prices, took the land of the poor, or seized it by force, and they worked great estates with bought slaves in place of free farmers. The free men of Italy, who were also its soldiers, grew fewer, and the country was filled with slaves.

Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus, chapter 8 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 2. Suppose slaves had been scarce and costly after the wars. Using this excerpt and Lesson 31.1, explain how that might have changed what happened to Roman farmers, and why the Gracchi might still have found a problem to fix.

assignments.title: 31.2 Primary Source Exercise: Sallust, The Jugurthine War
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Jugurtha left the city. It is said that as he went he often looked back at it in silence, and at last he said, "A city for sale, and soon to perish if it finds a buyer."

Before the destruction of Carthage, the Roman people and the Senate managed the state peacefully among themselves, and there was no struggle for glory or power. Fear of the enemy kept the citizens in good conduct. But when that fear had left their minds, the things that good fortune loves, license and pride, began to grow.

Sallust, The Jugurthine War, chapters 35 and 41 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Sallust was a Roman who wrote many decades after the war.

Question 1. Sallust says fear of Carthage kept Romans honest and that after Carthage fell, license and pride grew. Explain his argument, then use Lessons 31.1 and 31.2 to give one example from each lesson that fits it, and one point where you think the argument is too simple.

Question 2. Sallust says Jugurtha is said to have called Rome a city for sale, yet Sallust could not have heard it himself, and he wrote sharply about greed among the nobles. Explain how far you would trust the quotation, and what the story could still tell us even if the words are not exact. Use what you learned in Lesson 31.2 to support your answer.

assignments.title: 32.1 Critical Questions: Plutarch, Life of Crassus
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Crassus bought houses that were burning, and the houses near them, since their owners would sell cheaply in fear. In this way he came to own a great part of Rome. He used to say that no man is rich who cannot support an army from his own income.

Plutarch, Life of Crassus, chapter 2 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 1. Crassus says no one is rich who cannot support an army from his own income. Using Lesson 32.1, explain what this shows about how money and armies were connected in the late Republic, and why that might worry the Senate.

Excerpt 2

Pompey, who came upon some of the runaways as they fled, wrote to the Senate that Crassus had beaten the slaves in open battle, but that he himself had pulled the war up by the roots.

Plutarch, Life of Crassus, chapter 11 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 2. Suppose Pompey had not written that letter. Using the excerpt and Lesson 32.1, explain what the letter shows about what the generals wanted from a victory, and how it might have changed the way Romans saw Pompey.

assignments.title: 32.2 Primary Source Exercise: Caesar, The Gallic War
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Caesar saw that the hill could not be taken by assault, so he ordered works to be built all around it. He had a ditch dug twenty feet wide with straight sides, and behind it a rampart with a wall and towers. When he learned that a great Gallic army was coming to relieve the hill, he ordered a second line of the same kind, facing outward, so that even a vast force could not surround his men.

Vercingetorix called a council and said that he had made the war not for his own needs but for the common freedom, and that since fortune must be yielded to, he offered himself to the Romans, to be put to death or handed over as they pleased. Caesar sat on the rampart in front of the camp, and the leaders were brought out, and Vercingetorix was handed over.

Caesar, The Gallic War, book 7, chapters 72 to 74 and 89 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Caesar wrote this account himself, and he calls himself Caesar.

Question 1. Explain what this passage shows about Caesar's skill, and about how he wants Romans to see him. Notice that he writes "Caesar" and not "I." Using Lesson 32.2, say what effect that might have on his Roman readers.

Question 2. Caesar reports a speech by his enemy Vercingetorix about the common freedom. Explain how far you would trust Caesar's report of it. Then name something about the cost of the war that Lesson 32.2 says this passage leaves out, and say what that tells us about reading a general's own account.

assignments.title: 33.1 Critical Questions: Plutarch and Caesar
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

When he came to the river Rubicon, which divides Gaul from Italy, he stopped. He began to think how great a step he was taking, and he stood in silence, weighing the choice, and spoke with the friends beside him. Then he said, "We can still turn back, but once we cross this little bridge, everything must be settled by the sword."

Plutarch, Life of Caesar, chapter 32 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Caesar long after these events.

Question 1. Plutarch says Caesar stopped at the river and talked over the choice with his friends. Using Lesson 33.1, explain what Caesar might have faced if he had turned back, and what this tells you about how much choice he really had.

Excerpt 2

Caesar called the soldiers together. He reminded them of the wrongs his enemies had done him, and said that the tribunes of the people, who had stood up for him, had been driven from the city by force. He asked them to defend the good name and honor of the general under whom, for nine years, they had served the state with great success.

Caesar, The Civil War, book 1, chapter 7 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Caesar wrote this account himself, and he calls himself Caesar.

Question 2. Caesar tells his soldiers that he is defending his honor and the rights of the tribunes. Using Lesson 33.1, explain why Caesar would want his readers to see the war this way, and how the Senate might say the same events should be understood.

assignments.title: 33.2 Primary Source Exercise: Plutarch and Suetonius on Caesar
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Antony, who was one of the runners, made his way through the crowd and held out a crown wound with laurel. A few people clapped, and it was plain that they had been told to. When Caesar pushed it away, all the people applauded. Antony offered it again, and again only a few clapped, but when Caesar refused it, all applauded again. The trial, it seemed, had failed, and Caesar rose and ordered the crown carried to the Capitol.

He even let slip the saying that the Republic was nothing, a mere name without body or form.

Plutarch, Life of Caesar, chapter 61, and Suetonius, Life of the Deified Julius, chapter 77 (both adapted from public-domain translations). Both writers lived more than a century after Caesar's death.

Question 1. Plutarch says only a few people clapped when the crown was offered, and everyone clapped when Caesar refused it. Using Lesson 33.2, explain what this scene might tell us about how the crowd felt about kings, and name one thing about it that we cannot know.

Question 2. Suetonius says Caesar let slip that the Republic was a mere name. Explain how far you would trust this report, since Suetonius wrote long afterward and lived under emperors. Then use Lesson 33.2 to explain how such a saying would fit the reasons Brutus and Cassius gave for the killing, even if Caesar never said it.

assignments.title: 34.1 Critical Questions: Appian and Plutarch
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Whoever kills one of the proscribed and brings the head shall receive, if he is a free man, twenty-five thousand Attic drachmas. If he is a slave, he shall receive his freedom, ten thousand drachmas, and the citizen name of his master. The same rewards shall go to informers. Those who hide or help any of the proscribed shall themselves be put on the list.

Appian, Civil Wars, book 4, chapter 11 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Appian was a Greek who wrote about the Roman civil wars long after they ended.

Question 1. The edict offers money to free killers, freedom to slaves, and a threat to anyone who hides the proscribed. Using Lesson 34.1, explain what the Triumvirs hoped these rewards and threats would do to ordinary Romans, and what dangers came with them.

Excerpt 2

Antony ordered that Cicero's head and hands be cut off, the hands that had written the speeches against him. When they were brought, he looked on them with joy and laughed, and he ordered them fastened up above the speakers' platform in the Forum. The Romans shuddered at the sight, for they thought they saw not the face of Cicero, but an image of Antony's soul.

Plutarch, Life of Cicero, chapters 48 and 49 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Cicero about a hundred and fifty years after his death.

Question 2. Plutarch says the Romans shuddered when they saw Cicero's head and hands in the Forum. Using Lesson 34.1, explain why Antony wanted them put there, and what this display tells us about how the Republic had changed.

assignments.title: 34.2 Primary Source Exercise: Augustus, Res Gestae
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

At the age of nineteen, on my own decision and at my own cost, I raised an army, and with it I set free the Republic, which had been oppressed by the tyranny of a faction.

In my sixth and seventh consulships, when I had put an end to the civil wars, I handed the state over from my own power to the control of the Senate and the Roman people. For this service I was named Augustus by decree of the Senate. After that time I stood above all in influence, but I had no more power than the others who were my colleagues in each office.

Augustus, Res Gestae (Deeds of the Divine Augustus), chapters 1 and 34 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Augustus wrote this near the end of his life.

Question 1. Augustus says he handed the state back and had no more power than his colleagues. Using Lesson 34.2, explain what he gave up in 27 BC and what he kept, and say whether "no more power than the others" is a fair description.

Question 2. Augustus says that at nineteen he freed the Republic from "the tyranny of a faction." Using Lessons 34.1 and 34.2, name one thing about how he rose that this sentence leaves out. Then explain how far this makes you trust the text, and what it is still good evidence for.

assignments.title: 35.1 Critical Questions: Virgil and Juvenal
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Others, I believe, will shape bronze to breathe more softly and carve living faces from marble. They will plead in court better, and trace the paths of the sky and tell the rising stars. You, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with your power. These will be your arts: to set the custom of peace, to spare the conquered, and to beat down the proud.

Virgil, Aeneid, book 6, lines 847 to 853 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Virgil was a Roman poet who wrote in the time of Augustus.

Question 1. Virgil says that Rome's arts are to set the custom of peace, to spare the conquered, and to beat down the proud. Using Lesson 35.1, give one example of how Rome set the custom of peace in its provinces. Then say what a person living in a province might add to Virgil's list.

Excerpt 2

The people who once gave out commands, high office, legions, everything, now hold back and eagerly wish for only two things: bread and circus games.

Juvenal, Satire 10, lines 77 to 81 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Juvenal was a Roman poet who mocked the faults of his city, about a century after Augustus.

Question 2. Juvenal complains that the people who once gave out commands and offices now care only for bread and games. Using Lessons 28.2 and 35.1, explain what the Roman people had once done in the Republic, why rulers were glad to give them bread and games, and what this shows about the change from Republic to empire.

assignments.title: 35.2 Primary Source Exercise: Tacitus, Agricola
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Calgacus said: "Robbers of the world, they have taken everything, and now that the land has nothing left for them they search the sea. If an enemy is rich, they are greedy. If he is poor, they want glory. East and West have not satisfied them. To plunder, to butcher, to steal, they falsely call empire, and where they make a desert, they call it peace."

Little by little the Britons were led to the things that make people soft: the colonnades, the baths, and the elegant dinner party. The simple natives called this "civilization," when it was part of their slavery.

Tacitus, Agricola, chapters 30 and 21 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Tacitus was a Roman historian and the son-in-law of Agricola, the Roman general in Britain.

Question 1. Tacitus was the son-in-law of the Roman general in Britain, yet he wrote this speech for a British chief. Using Lesson 35.2, explain how far you would trust that these are Calgacus's real words, and what Tacitus might have wanted his Roman readers to think about.

Question 2. Lesson 35.1 says Rome governed with a light touch and that baths were public places to relax. Using Tacitus's second paragraph and Lessons 35.1 and 35.2, explain how the same baths and towns might look different to a Roman and to a Briton, and name one thing we still could not know.

assignments.title: 36.1 Critical Questions: Pliny and Trajan
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

They said that the whole of their guilt or error was this: they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and sing a hymn to Christ as to a god, and to bind themselves by an oath, not to do any wicked deed, but not to commit theft, robbery, or adultery, not to break their word, and not to refuse to return a deposit when asked.

Pliny the Younger, Letters, book 10, letter 96 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Pliny was a Roman governor writing to the emperor Trajan from a province in what is now Turkey, about AD 112.

Question 1. Pliny reports what the Christians told him about their meetings, and he found nothing worse. Using Lesson 36.1, explain what Pliny still asked them to do, and why that was a test of loyalty and not of crime.

Excerpt 2

You have followed the right course in your examination of these cases. No fixed rule can be laid down. They are not to be hunted out. If they are brought before you and the charge is proved, they must be punished. But if anyone denies that he is a Christian and proves it by worshiping our gods, he is to be pardoned, however suspect his past.

Trajan to Pliny, Letters, book 10, letter 97 (adapted from a public-domain translation). This is the emperor's reply.

Question 2. Suppose Trajan had ordered governors to hunt down Christians in every town. Using his actual reply and Lesson 36.1, explain how things might have been different for Christians, and why Trajan may have chosen not to give that order.

assignments.title: 36.2 Primary Source Exercise: Lactantius and Eusebius
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Constantine was warned in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on the shields of his soldiers, and so to go into battle. He did as he was told. With a slanting letter X, its top bent round, he marked the name of Christ on their shields. Armed with this sign, his army took up their swords.

He said that about the middle of the day, when the sun was beginning to turn, he saw with his own eyes the sign of a cross of light in the sky, above the sun, and with it the words, "By this, conquer." He said that he and the whole army with him were amazed. He doubted at first what the sign could mean. Then, in the night, Christ appeared to him with the same sign, and told him to make a copy of it and use it as a protection against his enemies.

Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 44, and Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 1, chapters 28 and 29 (both adapted from public-domain translations). Both writers were Christians who wrote soon after the events, and Eusebius says Constantine told him the story himself, long afterward.

Question 1. Compare the two accounts. Name one thing they agree on and one thing they tell differently. Then use Lesson 36.2 to explain why a historian cannot simply choose the account that sounds best.

Question 2. Eusebius says Constantine told him the story himself, long afterward. Explain how that might make the story more believable and how it might make it less believable. Then use Lesson 36.2 to say what Constantine's later actions add to the question of whether he truly believed.

quizzes.title: 19.1 Reading Quiz: Mountains and Sea

questions.text: In Egypt and Mesopotamia, strong rulers gathered many towns under one crown. Why was that much harder to do in Greece?

answers.text: Greek farmers refused to pay taxes to any ruler, so no king could afford an army.
Mountains and islands split the land into small areas, with no wide plains for an army to cross.
Greece had too few people to fill an army, so no ruler could ever march far.
The Greeks spoke so many different languages that no single ruler could give orders to all of them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Egypt and Mesopotamia grew up on wide river plains where a ruler could march an army across flat ground. Greece was cut into valleys and islands, so each place went its own way. The Greeks did share a language, so the last choice fails.

questions.text: A Greek traveler would say, "I am a citizen of Corinth," not "I am a citizen of Greece." What does this best show?

answers.text: Greeks did not care about their gods or festivals, and they trusted only their own families.
Greeks were ashamed of belonging to a country that had no strong king to rule it.
Corinth was the largest and richest city in all of Greece, so people were proud to say it.
A person's loyalty belonged first to his own city-state, not to a larger country.

questions.feedback_general: The Greeks shared a language, gods, and festivals, but not one government. Each polis guarded its own freedom, so people named their city as their home and their loyalty.

questions.text: Hesiod quarreled with his brother over land and then wrote a poem praising justice. What can we infer about why he valued justice?

answers.text: He had seen how much a farmer needs fair judges and honest neighbors in order to prosper.
He wanted to become a famous warrior like Achilles.
He believed that only kings could be fair.
He thought justice mattered less than glory.

questions.feedback_general: Hesiod was a small farmer who felt cheated in a land dispute. He believed cities with fair judges would prosper and cities with crooked judges would suffer. Homer's heroes, not Hesiod, chased glory.

questions.text: Hoplites bought their own armor. Why might a farmer-soldier begin to ask for a voice in running his city?

answers.text: The heavy armor made him too weak and slow to farm, so he needed help from the city.
He was a noble who hoped to use the city's soldiers to make himself a king.
He risked his life and paid his own costs for the city, so he felt he had earned a say.
The city law required every hoplite to take a seat in the government as soon as he came home.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says men who fought for the city often began to ask for a voice in running it, though this was never guaranteed and did not happen the same way everywhere. Fighting at one's own expense gave a farmer a reason to expect a share.

questions.text: Settlers from a Greek city found a colony in Sicily. Which description best fits the new colony?

answers.text: A province governed directly by officials from the mother city.
A new polis with its own laws and citizens that often kept friendly ties with the mother city.
A temporary camp that was abandoned after a year.
A city ruled by the king of Persia.

questions.feedback_general: A colony was usually independent, with its own laws and citizens, though it often kept ties of friendship and religion with the mother city. This is how Greek ways of life spread around the Mediterranean.

quizzes.title: 19.2 Reading Quiz: Sparta, a Polis Built for War

questions.text: Sparta took both the land and the people of Messenia. What does this tell us about the Spartans' situation afterward?

answers.text: They became the richest traders in Greece, since they now controlled the busy Messenian harbors.
They no longer needed an army, because Messenia had been the only enemy within reach.
They freed the Messenians within a few years and asked them to join the Spartan army.
They lived among a large population they ruled by force and had to watch for revolt.

questions.feedback_general: The helots far outnumbered their Spartan masters, so Sparta lived in constant fear of a rising. Many historians think that fear shaped nearly every Spartan rule.

questions.text: Sparta had two kings, a council of elders, five overseers, and an assembly. What was the likely purpose of dividing power so many ways?

answers.text: To make sure that no single person or group could grab all the power.
To give the helots a chance to vote on the laws and elect the kings.
To let every person in the Spartan lands take part equally in running the state.
To avoid ever having to fight a war, since the kings could not agree on one.

questions.feedback_general: Each part could slow down the others. Kings led the army but the overseers watched them, and the elders shaped the laws but the assembly could say yes or no. The helots and perioikoi had no vote.

questions.text: Why would a city that feared revolt raise its boys in the harsh agoge?

answers.text: Spartans did not value family life.
It needed soldiers who would obey without question and hold their place in the line.
The boys needed to learn how to farm Messenia.
The city wanted to teach its boys to seek personal glory above all.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a city that fears revolt needs soldiers who obey. Spartans believed hardship made strong men, and strong men made a safe city. A Spartan was taught to put the city first, unlike Homer's glory-seeking heroes.

questions.text: The Spartiates did not farm or trade. Which fact from the lesson best explains how they were free to train for war?

answers.text: Iron bars served as money, which made trading with outsiders slow.
Spartan women ran the city while the men were away at war for years at a time.
Helots farmed the land and perioikoi made goods and traded.
The kings paid each citizen a yearly salary out of the treasury of Delphi.

questions.feedback_general: Because the helots farmed and the perioikoi made things, the Spartiates were free to train. The iron money was a separate fact about how Sparta discouraged trade.

questions.text: The lesson compares Sparta to a club with a very small membership. Which sentence best explains the comparison?

answers.text: Most people in the Spartan lands had no vote or share in ruling the state.
Anyone could join Sparta by paying a fee, but few people could afford the price.
Sparta welcomed strangers and gave them citizenship after a short period of training.
Sparta had a very large citizen body, and most men in the lands were members.

questions.feedback_general: Only full Spartiates took part in the assembly. The perioikoi and helots lived in the Spartan lands with no voice. Sparta had answered how to defend a polis, but not who should share in ruling it.

quizzes.title: 20.1 Reading Quiz: Solon Weakens the Athenian Aristocracy

questions.text: Why did the debt crisis push Athens close to civil war?

answers.text: Foreign armies were about to invade, and the city leaders could not agree on how to defend it.
Citizens were being made slaves for debt, and the poor were angry while the rich were afraid.
The nobles wanted to give all of the land to the poor, but the farmers refused to take it.
The Areopagus had been abolished, and no court was left to judge the quarrels.

questions.feedback_general: A farmer who could not repay a loan could be seized and sold as a slave. The lesson says a city cannot hold together when citizens become slaves of their neighbors.

questions.text: The poor asked Solon to divide the land of the rich equally. He refused. What does this suggest about Solon?

answers.text: He was secretly on the side of the nobles.
He wanted to give everything the poor asked for.
He tried to stay between the two sides, giving neither all it wanted.
He did not understand what the poor wanted.

questions.feedback_general: Solon said he stood between the two sides like a boundary stone. Both sides trusted him partly because he was fair to each and gave neither everything.

questions.text: Before Solon, birth decided who could rule. After Solon, wealth did. Why did this change matter?

answers.text: A rich man from a non-noble family could now rise, so more people had a stake in the city.
It made the aristocracy stronger than before, since nobles still held every single high office.
It gave the thetes the right to hold the highest offices and to lead the army.
It ended the Assembly, so rich men alone made every decision for the city.

questions.feedback_general: The old aristocracy was weakened but not abolished. A man who could rise by the work of his farm had more reason to care about the laws. The thetes could attend the Assembly and sit on a jury, but not hold office.

questions.text: Why did the thetes, who could hold no office, still gain something under Solon?

answers.text: They received free land taken from the rich nobles, which made them small farmers like the hoplites.
They became hoplites, because the city now paid for their armor and spears.
They could choose the archons each year, though they could not hold the office.
They could attend the Assembly and sit on a jury that heard appeals, a small voice.

questions.feedback_general: Aristotle says the laborers could attend the Assembly and sit on a jury that heard appeals. This mattered because it gave the poorest citizens a small voice.

questions.text: Peisistratus kept Solon's laws, lent money to poor farmers, and built temples, yet he was still called a tyrant. What does this show about the Greek word?

answers.text: A tyrant was always a cruel man who ruled by fear and used spies against his people.
A tyrant was a man who took power by force, whether or not he ruled harshly.
A tyrant was chosen by the Assembly for a term of ten years, and then he was sent home again.
A tyrant was a member of the Areopagus who had been chosen by the other nobles.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the word did not always mean a cruel man. A tyrant took power by force, and even a mild one took away the people's freedom to decide.

quizzes.title: 20.2 Reading Quiz: Cleisthenes Invents Democracy

questions.text: Sparta helped to drive Hippias out of Athens. What does the lesson mean when it calls this ironic?

answers.text: Sparta wanted Hippias to stay in power, and the Athenians forced him out against Sparta's will.
Sparta helped free Athens, yet Athens would grow into Sparta's rival.
Sparta gained control of Athens, and for many years Athens paid tribute to the Spartans.
Hippias was a Spartan king sent to rule Athens by the council.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson notes that Sparta helped free Athens while helping to make a rival. It is an example of events having results no one planned.

questions.text: When Cleisthenes was losing his quarrel with Isagoras, he brought the common people into his party. Why was this bold?

answers.text: Nobles could not speak to common people, and the law forbade any nobleman from asking their help.
The people were all supporters of Isagoras, so Cleisthenes was asking his rival's friends to join him.
Nobles usually settled such fights among themselves, and the people might not give power back.
It was against the law of Sparta, and Sparta would punish any city that tried it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says nobles usually kept their quarrels among themselves. Once ordinary Athenians had helped decide a struggle, they would expect to keep a voice.

questions.text: Why did Cleisthenes make each tribe a mix of people from the city, the coast, and the inland country?

answers.text: So that each tribe could be ruled by the noble families of its own region, as in the old days.
So that no noble family could control a region, and men would think of themselves as Athenians.
So that each region would have its own army and could defend itself without help from the others.
So that the poorest citizens would be left out of the tribes and kept out of the Assembly as well.

questions.feedback_general: Before, a noble could count on men of his own region to follow him. Mixed tribes meant a man from the coast worked beside a man from the city and the hills, and a shared loyalty helped hold the city together.

questions.text: Council members were chosen by lot, which means by drawing names. What does this method suggest about who could serve?

answers.text: Only men from noble families could serve, since the rest were thought unfit to rule.
Only the wisest man in each tribe could serve, as judged by the old Areopagus.
Only men who had served in the army for ten years could serve on the Council.
Any citizen in the tribe had a chance to serve, not only the powerful.

questions.feedback_general: Fifty men from each tribe were chosen by lot to prepare business for the Assembly. Service did not depend on birth or power.

questions.text: The lesson says a good student of history holds two thoughts about Athens at once. Which pair matches the lesson?

answers.text: Athens was a perfect city, and yet it was ruined by the freedom it gave its citizens.
Athens made ordinary citizens part of ruling, and it left most people who lived there out.
Athens had no democracy at all, and yet it still had a great many slaves and foreigners living inside its walls.
Athens was weak against its enemies, and it was loved by Sparta for that very reason.

questions.feedback_general: Only free men born in Athens counted as citizens. Women, slaves, and foreigners living in the city were left out. Both the new achievement and the limits are true.

quizzes.title: 21.1 Reading Quiz: The Ionian Revolt and Darius's Revenge

questions.text: Herodotus says Aristagoras began the revolt after his attack on Naxos failed. What does this suggest about his reasons?

answers.text: He was mainly guided by a plan to bring Athenian democracy to all of the Persian empire.
He acted from fear for his own safety and from ambition, not from a grand plan.
He was ordered to revolt by the Spartans, who had promised to send him ships.
He wanted to give Miletus to Athens as a gift in return for ships and men.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the revolt began from fear and ambition. Historians study the choices of individuals because small decisions can start great chains of events.

questions.text: Sparta refused to help the Ionians and Athens agreed. What best explains the difference in the lesson?

answers.text: Athens had no army at all, so the Athenians needed allies in order to defend themselves.
Sparta was a friend of Persia and had signed a treaty with Darius many years before.
The Spartan king heard that Persia was far inland, but the Athenian Assembly said yes.
Athens had been conquered by Persia already, and so the Athenians wished to take revenge.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartan king refused because of the distance. The Athenian Assembly had been working for only a few years under Cleisthenes and voted to send twenty ships.

questions.text: Athens withdrew after the burning of Sardis and took no further part in the revolt. Why did Darius still want revenge on Athens?

answers.text: To punish Athens for burning Sardis and to stop any Greek city from helping his subjects again.
Athens had taken the Persian throne and refused to give it back to the royal family of Persia, as the Persians demanded.
Athens had refused to trade with Persia and had closed its harbors to Persian ships.
Athens had killed his father in battle, and Darius had sworn an oath to avenge him.

questions.feedback_general: To Darius, Athens had joined his enemies and burned a city of his empire. He also wanted to make sure no Greek city would help his subjects rebel again.

questions.text: The lesson says Darius could not see the future. How does that detail help explain his decision?

answers.text: He knew Marathon would be a defeat.
He had already lost a war with Athens.
He expected a quick victory over one small city after crushing an empire's rebels.
He was too old to lead an army.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson explains that Darius expected an easy win. Understanding what people expected, not what we know came next, helps us see why they chose as they did.

questions.text: The Ionians lived inside the Persian empire but shared a language and gods with the Greeks across the sea. How did this help bring the two worlds into war?

answers.text: The Ionians had no interest in Greek affairs and wished only to be left alone by both sides in peace.
Persia and Greece had never met before the Ionians introduced the two peoples.
The Ionians were forbidden to trade with either side, and so they began a revolt.
Being between two worlds put them in a hard spot, and their revolt pulled Athens into the conflict.

questions.feedback_general: The Ionians had the culture of free Greek cities and the duties of Persian subjects. Their revolt came out of that tension and linked the two worlds.

quizzes.title: 21.2 Reading Quiz: Marathon

questions.text: The vote of the ten Athenian generals was tied. What was the effect of the war leader's vote?

answers.text: It ended the Persian war.
It brought Sparta to Marathon.
It decided that Athens would march out and fight instead of waiting inside the walls.
It chose Hippias as king.

questions.feedback_general: Callimachus cast the deciding vote for battle. The lesson says a single vote may have decided the fate of Athens.

questions.text: Sparta arrived only after the battle because of a religious festival. Why does the lesson call this a place where history turns on a small thing?

answers.text: The Spartans did not want to help Athens and used the festival as an excuse to stay home.
If the festival had fallen on another date, Sparta might have fought beside Athens.
The festival was held in Athens that year, so the Spartans were forced to stay away.
Athens was not allowed to ask for help during the festival, so the Spartans could not come.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartans agreed to help but would not march until the moon was full. Contingency means events can turn on small facts like a date.

questions.text: Why did the Greeks choose to camp at the foot of the hills at Marathon?

answers.text: They wanted to be near their ships, so they could escape if the battle turned.
Persian horsemen, the king's strongest force, could not easily reach them there.
The hills were sacred ground, so no Persian dared to fight near them.
They hoped to hide from the Persians until the Spartans arrived.

questions.feedback_general: The Battle callout says the Greeks camped at the foot of the hills, where Persian horsemen could not easily reach them. The Persians kept their ships on the beach.

questions.text: Heavily armed Greeks beat lighter-armed Persians at close range. Which detail from the lesson best supports this?

answers.text: The Persians had no ships and had to march all the way around the Aegean Sea to Marathon.
The Greeks had archers on the hills who shot down the Persians as they landed.
The Greeks trained to fight shoulder to shoulder, with heavy armor and long spears.
The Persians were not allowed to fight at Marathon because of a religious rule.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson ties the victory to the phalanx. Hoplites wore heavy armor and long spears, and each man trusted the man beside him. The Persians wore lighter gear with shorter spears and bows.

questions.text: The lesson calls the story of the runner who died after announcing the victory a legend. What does that label tell you?

answers.text: The story was written down by Herodotus himself, who saw the runner collapse in the marketplace.
The story is proven false by archaeology, since no road ever ran from Marathon to the city of Athens.
The story is about Pheidippides, who ran to Athens to ask for help before the battle.
The story comes from later centuries and is not in our main source, so historians call it a legend.

questions.feedback_general: Herodotus never mentions the run to announce the victory. He tells instead of Pheidippides' run to Sparta. Careful historians tell the legend but mark it as one.

quizzes.title: 22.1 Reading Quiz: The 300 Spartans at Thermopylae

questions.text: Xerxes had a canal dug at Mount Athos and bridges built across the Hellespont. What do these preparations suggest?

answers.text: He expected an easy, quick march across Greece with little need for any preparation.
He wanted to attack Persia's own cities and needed a way to reach them by water.
He was planning the invasion with great care and fully expected to win the war.
He did not intend to enter Greece, but only to frighten the Greek cities into paying him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says everything about the plan said Persia meant to win. The canal avoided rough water where an earlier fleet was wrecked, and the bridges let armies cross on foot.

questions.text: Sparta was given command of the Greek alliance even though Athens had the biggest fleet. What can we infer?

answers.text: Sparta had the best soldiers, and Athens had to set aside pride for unity.
Athens had no ships at all, so the Spartans were chosen by default to lead the fleet.
Sparta had joined the Persians, and the other cities chose to give it command as a trick.
Corinth had been given command because its harbor lay nearest.

questions.feedback_general: Choosing Sparta made sense because it had the best land soldiers. The lesson says this showed how much Athens had to give up for the sake of unity.

questions.text: Why was the pass at Thermopylae a good place for a small Greek force to stand?

answers.text: It was close to Athens, so the Greeks could easily bring more soldiers and supplies.
It was where the Persian fleet was anchored, so the Greek army could attack the ships.
The pass was full of Greek allies who had already been waiting there for many months.
The road was only wide enough for a few men, so Persia could not use its numbers.

questions.feedback_general: In a narrow pass only a few men can fight at a time. The lesson says the place did as much work as the men.

questions.text: Leonidas sent most of the allies away when he learned the Persians were behind him. What does this choice show?

answers.text: He wanted to hold the pass as long as he could so that others could escape.
He was afraid to fight and hoped to slip away before the Persians came.
He wanted to surrender to Xerxes and hoped the king would spare the Spartans in return.
He did not understand the danger and thought the Persian army was only a small force.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Leonidas could have run but chose to stay. Courage of this kind is a virtue the Greeks admired and history remembers.

questions.text: The Greeks lost the pass. Which statement best explains why the lesson still treats Thermopylae as important?

answers.text: Xerxes turned back after the battle, because his army had lost so many men in the narrow pass.
The stand showed Greeks would die rather than submit, and it inspired later courage.
Leonidas escaped through the mountains and went on to win the war for the Greeks.
The fleet at Artemisium won a clear victory on the same days that the army fought.

questions.feedback_general: Artemisium was not decided. The value of Thermopylae lay in the time gained for evacuating Athens and preparing the fleet, and in the story told afterward.

quizzes.title: 22.2 Reading Quiz: Salamis and Plataea

questions.text: Athens spent the silver from the Laurion mines on ships, not on dividing the money among citizens. What was one lasting result?

answers.text: The city no longer needed soldiers, since ships alone could now defend all of Attica.
The thetes, the poorest citizens, rowed the fleet and gained a new role in defending Athens.
The Acropolis was protected from fire, because stone walls were built around the hill.
Sparta joined Athens in a lasting alliance, and the two cities shared the same fleet.

questions.feedback_general: A trireme needed about two hundred men to row it, and the rowers were the thetes. A role in defending the city helped give them a bigger voice in governing it.

questions.text: Why did Themistocles want to fight in the narrow strait at Salamis?

answers.text: The Persian fleet could not use its larger numbers in such a narrow space.
The Greeks had no ships that could sail in open water, only small river boats.
Xerxes had sent word that he would only fight in the strait, and Themistocles agreed.
Sparta demanded it, because its generals wanted the war far from the Peloponnese.

questions.feedback_general: In a narrow space the huge Persian fleet jammed together, and Greek triremes rammed them one by one.

questions.text: Why did Themistocles' trick against Xerxes work?

answers.text: Xerxes could not read the message, and so he followed the advice of his own captains.
The Greeks outnumbered the Persians, and Xerxes feared to wait for them to attack.
Xerxes wanted to believe the Greeks were afraid and that a quick victory was near.
Xerxes had no ships left, so he was ready to believe any offer the Greeks made.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the trick worked because Xerxes wanted to believe it. An enemy's hopes can be used against him.

questions.text: At Plataea, Spartans, Athenians, and soldiers of many other cities fought together. Why does the lesson say this deserves to be remembered?

answers.text: It was the first time the Spartans ever fought a battle outside their own lands.
It ended the Olympic Games, which were never held again after the battle.
Athens had no part in it, and so the credit belongs to Sparta alone.
It was rare for Greeks from so many different cities to fight side by side.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls this unity rare in the story. Many Greek cities sided with Persia or stayed out, and quarrels never fully stopped.

questions.text: What does the lesson suggest about Greek unity after the Persian danger passed?

answers.text: The Greeks stayed united for centuries and fought every later war side by side.
Old rivalries came back, as proud Athens and suspicious Sparta drifted apart.
Sparta became the ruler of all Greece, and the other cities obeyed its commands.
The cities joined into one country, with a single government that met in Athens.

questions.feedback_general: The closing says the Greeks did not stay united for long. The same forces that nearly lost the war would return.

quizzes.title: 23.1 Reading Quiz: From Delian League to Athenian Empire

questions.text: Most league members stopped sending ships and sent tribute instead. How did this help Athens become an empire?

answers.text: Athens used the money to build more ships, while members had no navy to resist it.
Members grew stronger than Athens, since they now kept the money for themselves.
The league moved to Sparta, which then used the tribute to pay its own army.
Members began to elect Athenian leaders to their councils, so Athens gained a right to rule them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Athens used the tribute to build more ships. A member that tried to leave, like Naxos or Thasos, was forced to stay.

questions.text: The lesson says that to members, Athens stopped being a partner and became a master. Which detail best supports this?

answers.text: The league treasury was kept on Delos, an island sacred to Apollo.
Athens led because it had the biggest fleet, and the members agreed to this.
Members still had to pay, but they were not allowed to leave the league.
Athens fought Persia for many years, and the members admired its courage.

questions.feedback_general: At first the league was a bargain. Once the danger faded, members were still paying and could not leave. Moving the treasury to Athens around 454 BC underlines the change.

questions.text: When Ephialtes took powers from the old council, who gained them?

answers.text: The kings of Sparta, who sent officials to Athens to hold the powers for a few years.
Cimon and his friends, who were the leaders of the noble families and had many ships.
The archons, who were chosen by lot each year and so took over the powers of the council.
The Assembly and the people's jury courts, which were open to ordinary citizens.

questions.feedback_general: In 462 BC the powers went to the Assembly and the jury courts, so the people had the final word. The rowers who saved Athens at Salamis could argue they had earned a larger share.

questions.text: Why were many officials chosen by lot and paid for jury service under Pericles?

answers.text: To keep the poor out of government, since paid officials would be controlled by the rich.
So that anyone had a chance to serve, and a poor man could afford to take part.
To make the courts shorter, since jurors paid by the day wanted to go home early.
To pay for the navy, since the jury money was taken from the fleet's treasury.

questions.feedback_general: Lot meant no one could buy an office. Pay meant a poor man could afford to serve. Many citizens learned how government worked.

questions.text: Athens gave more of its citizens a real part in ruling than Sparta did. What does the lesson still say about both cities?

answers.text: Both ruled without any slaves, and relied on free citizens to do all the work.
Both kept most of the people living in their lands out of any share in power.
Both had kings who ruled for life and were chosen from a single family.
Both let women vote in the Assembly, though only if their husbands agreed.

questions.feedback_general: Athenian citizens were free men with Athenian parents. Women, slaves, and metics were left out. Sparta also kept most people out of power.

quizzes.title: 23.2 Reading Quiz: The Parthenon and the Theater of Dionysus

questions.text: Pericles' enemies said Athens decorated itself with other people's money. What was that quarrel about?

answers.text: Whether Phidias was a good enough sculptor to be trusted with so much marble.
How far a ruling city may spend the wealth that it takes from those it rules.
Whether marble was too costly for a city that was still at war with Persia.
Whether plays should be allowed in a city that was still recovering from war.

questions.feedback_general: Part of the money came from tribute paid by allies. Pericles answered that Athens had done the work of defending Greece.

questions.text: A choregos paid for a chorus as a duty to the city. How did this put the Greek love of honor to public use?

answers.text: A rich man won glory by serving the city, so private ambition fed public pride.
It kept rich men from taking part in festivals, so that only the poor could attend.
It let the poor avoid paying taxes, and the rich paid for all of the public festivals.
It ended competition among playwrights, since every chorus was paid for by the city.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson contrasts this with the Homeric hero, whose glory belonged to one man. Here the old love of contest served the community.

questions.text: Antigone buries her brother against the king's order. What question does the play force the audience to face?

answers.text: Whether Athens should build a navy against Persia and Sparta.
Whether a duty to one's family can ever outweigh the law of the state.
Whether Persia should be invaded by the Greeks, now that the old war was over.
Whether tribute should be paid by the cities that had joined the Delian League.

questions.feedback_general: The play offers no simple answer. The lesson says such plays gave the whole city a chance to think about justice and duty together.

questions.text: A free city let Aristophanes mock its leaders in front of nearly twenty thousand people. What does this suggest about Athens?

answers.text: Athens ruled by fear, and punished anyone who dared to speak against the city.
Athens had no real theater, and so people watched plays in the open market.
Athens allowed open criticism of its own leaders and thinkers, even in public.
Athens hated comedy, and the plays were kept short for that reason.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson uses this to show that a free city let a playwright make fun of its own leaders, including thinkers like Socrates.

questions.text: Herodotus told stories with wonder, and Thucydides was stern and looked for causes. What did they give us together?

answers.text: A habit of asking what happened and why, by checking sources and finding causes.
A single story about the gods, told in the same way by every Greek city.
A list of Athenian laws, with the dates on which each one had been passed.
A map of Persia, drawn from the notes that both men made on their travels.

questions.feedback_general: Before them the past was mostly told as myth or praise. The lesson says that habit is still the heart of history.

quizzes.title: 24.1 Reading Quiz: The Road to War

questions.text: Thucydides called the growth of Athenian power, and the fear it caused in Sparta, the truest cause of the war. What does this suggest about why the war began?

answers.text: Athens had attacked Sparta without any warning, and Sparta could only strike back in anger.
Corcyra had asked Sparta for help against Athens, and the Spartans felt bound to answer.
Sparta felt threatened as Athens grew stronger, even though Athens had not attacked it.
The cities of the Peloponnesian League wanted to join Athens, and Sparta tried to stop them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Sparta did not need to be attacked to feel afraid. It was enough that Athens kept growing stronger. The quarrels at Corcyra, Potidaea, and Megara were the sparks, not the deepest cause.

questions.text: Athens made a defensive alliance with Corcyra and sent a small fleet. What was Athens most likely trying to prevent?

answers.text: Corinth gaining the large Corcyraean fleet, which would have shifted the balance at sea.
Corcyra paying tribute to Sparta every year and joining the Peloponnesian League with it.
Corinth asking Athens to protect it from the Corcyraeans and from the Spartan army.
Its own people moving to the island of Corcyra and leaving the city without defenders.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Athens did not want Corinth to gain Corcyra's ships. Corinth was an ally of Sparta and was furious, which is how a quarrel between two colonies became part of a larger crisis.

questions.text: Pericles told the Athenians to give up their land, move behind the Long Walls, and trust the sea. What did this plan depend on most?

answers.text: Spartan soldiers running out of food before the winter, so that they would have to go home.
Athenian hoplites beating the Spartans in an open field once the Spartans grew tired.
Persian help against the Spartan army, which the king had promised in exchange for tribute.
Athens keeping control of the sea so that grain ships could still reach Piraeus.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Athens could not be starved out while its fleet kept the grain ships coming. If Athens lost the sea, the plan would fail. Athens could not beat the Spartans in an open field, which is why Pericles avoided one.

questions.text: Pericles asked farmers to watch their fields burn and not fight back. Why was this plan so hard to follow?

answers.text: The Long Walls were too small to hold anyone, so most farmers had no place to go.
It asked proud citizens to accept real losses without striking back, and many wanted to fight.
The farmers did not know where Piraeus was, and no one had shown them the road.
Sparta never burned any fields, so the plan made no sense to the people of Athens.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the plan was sound but asked a great deal. Farmers saw smoke from their own burning fields and were told to do nothing. Pericles held them back, though not everyone loved him for it.

questions.text: Beyond the deaths it caused, what does Thucydides say the plague did to Athens?

answers.text: It made the Athenians trust their leaders more, since Pericles himself never fell ill from it.
It sent the Spartan army home for good, because the soldiers feared that they would catch it.
It weakened people's respect for law and the gods, because many thought they might be dead tomorrow.
It showed the doctors how to cure the fever, and Athens became known for its healers.

questions.feedback_general: Thucydides says people began to lose their fear of the laws and of the gods. A city is held together by habits of duty and self-control, and when those fail the damage lasts longer than the sickness.

quizzes.title: 24.2 Reading Quiz: How Athens Lost the War

questions.text: At Melos, the Athenians argued that right and wrong matter only between equals. What danger does Thucydides want his readers to notice in that argument?

answers.text: Melos would soon be stronger than Athens, and the argument would then be turned against Athens.
Sparta had no reason to care about small islands, so Melos had no one to turn to for help.
The Athenian speakers were poor at arguing, so they lost the debate and the island as well.
If the strong may do whatever they can, then no city is safe when it is the weaker one.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that if the strong may do whatever they can, no city is safe, not even Athens. Thucydides lets the story speak for itself and says that the next year Athens would learn that the strong do not always stay strong.

questions.text: Nicias warned that Sicily was too far away and the cost too high. Why was the expedition such a risky gamble?

answers.text: Sicily had no harbors that Athens could use, so the ships had no place to land and rest.
It was a very long sail from home, supplies were hard to send, and Athens staked its whole fleet.
Syracuse was already an ally of Athens, so the fleet would be sailing against its own friends.
Athens had no money to pay for any ships, so the fleet had to be built with borrowed gold.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson stresses that food and supplies had to cross a long stretch of sea, and that any mistake would be costly. An attack there was a gamble with the city's whole fleet.

questions.text: Alcibiades was called home for trial, ran away to Sparta, and advised the Spartans. What can we infer from this?

answers.text: Sparta had no interest in what Athens was doing, and Alcibiades had to work hard to change that.
Alcibiades had been loyal to Sparta since boyhood, and so his flight was no real surprise.
A city can be badly hurt when a gifted man it has turned against goes over to its enemy.
The Spartans did not take his advice, and he soon had to flee to the Persian court.

questions.feedback_general: Alcibiades told Sparta to send a commander to Syracuse and to fortify a place inside Athenian land. Sparta did both. The lesson says this helped bring the expedition down and kept Athens under pressure all year long.

questions.text: Sparta had fought Persia at Thermopylae, yet later took Persian gold. What did the gold give Sparta?

answers.text: A fleet and crews, which Sparta had always lacked.
Better hoplites than Athens could train, since the gold paid for years of full-time drill.
The Long Walls of Athens, which Persian engineers helped the Spartans to pull down.
A peace that lasted fifty years.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Spartans had never before been a sea power. With Persian money they built a fleet, and Lysander got still more money from a Persian prince. In return, Persia wanted the Greek cities of Asia Minor.

questions.text: At Aegospotami, Lysander captured almost every Athenian ship. What mistake made this possible?

answers.text: The Athenian ships were too slow to leave the harbor, so Lysander simply sailed in and took them.
Lysander had a much larger fleet than Athens, so the Athenians could not hope to fight back.
Alcibiades sailed over to the Spartans with the Athenian fleet and handed the ships to Lysander.
The Athenian crews went ashore for food and were scattered, and they ignored a warning to move.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Lysander sailed over while the crews were scattered on the shore. Alcibiades, who lived nearby, is said to have warned them, but they ignored him.

quizzes.title: 25.1 Reading Quiz: Socrates on Trial

questions.text: After the Thirty fell, Athenian citizens swore not to punish each other for what had been done during the war and the tyranny. What was the purpose of this amnesty?

answers.text: To heal the city and keep old quarrels from tearing it apart.
To bring the Thirty back into power once the people had grown tired of the new government.
To repay the debt that Athens owed to Sparta.
To punish everyone who had fought for the Thirty, so that no one would dare try it again.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the amnesty was meant to heal the city. It also had a side effect that matters later, because it may have shaped the charges brought against Socrates.

questions.text: The oracle at Delphi said that no one was wiser than Socrates, and he went looking for someone who was. What did he decide in the end?

answers.text: That he had read more books than anyone else in the city.
That he had won more battles than anyone else, since he had fought as a hoplite in the war.
That he was wiser only in one way: he knew that he did not know.
That the oracle had made a mistake, and that it should be ignored from then on by all Athenians.

questions.feedback_general: In Plato's account, Socrates questioned famous men and found that those who sounded certain could not explain their own words. He decided he was wiser only in this: he knew that he did not know.

questions.text: Anytus, one of the accusers, had fought against the Thirty. What does this suggest about the men who brought Socrates to court?

answers.text: They were secretly friends of Critias, and they used the trial to protect him from blame.
They may have honestly feared that his questions and his students had harmed the democracy.
They had been paid by Sparta to remove him, since he had spoken against the war.
They wanted Plato to rule Athens, and Socrates was the only man who stood in his way.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the accusers were not tyrants but democrats who loved their city. It was in some ways a trial of how far a democracy can allow questioning.

questions.text: Some historians think the charge about the gods was used to get around the amnesty. What is the reasoning?

answers.text: The jury cared only about religion, and so they would not have listened to any political charge.
Socrates had been a priest of Athens, so a charge about the gods would have been the easiest.
Plato had asked for a religious trial, because he thought it would help his teacher to win.
The amnesty barred charges for acts during the tyranny, so a different charge was needed to reach him.

questions.feedback_general: Critias and Alcibiades had been companions of Socrates, and many Athenians linked him to them. The amnesty meant no one could be tried for acts during the tyranny, so some historians think a religious charge was a way around that rule.

questions.text: Aristotle taught that human beings are made to live in a polis. Which statement would he be most likely to agree with?

answers.text: A person who could never live in any city would lose the chance to become fully good.
A person is best off living alone and far from other people, where no one can lead him astray.
Only rulers need to be good, because everyone else in the city simply has to obey them.
A city should care only for its richest citizens, because they pay for the festivals and the fleet.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Aristotle held that the polis is the only place where a person can fully become good. He also taught that any form of rule is good when it cares for the whole people and bad when it cares only for the rulers.

quizzes.title: 25.2 Reading Quiz: Sparta's Empire and Thebes's Moment

questions.text: Many Greek cities had been told that Sparta fought to set Greece free. Why did they come to hate Sparta within a few years?

answers.text: Sparta charged them higher taxes than Athens ever had, and the cities could not pay the bill.
Sparta put friendly oligarchs in power and placed garrisons in some cities, so it acted as a new master.
Sparta refused to fight against anyone, so the cities felt that they had been left alone.
Sparta gave every city a democracy, and the old rulers of those cities then turned against it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Spartan officers gave orders where Athenian ones had given them before. Spartiates had trained for war and not for ruling other people gently.

questions.text: Under the King's Peace, the Persian king told the Greeks where their borders lay. What does this show about the Greeks?

answers.text: Their quarrels let a foreign king decide matters they had once fought to defend.
They had defeated Persia again and demanded more land from the king in the east.
They no longer cared about their own cities and wished to be ruled from a single capital.
They had agreed to give up their language and to use the Persian tongue in all treaties.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that at Marathon and Salamis Greeks had fought so that Persia would not rule them. Now the Great King could tell them where their borders lay. They had won the war against Persia but lost the peace to their own quarrels.

questions.text: At Leuctra, Epaminondas packed his best men fifty rows deep and aimed them at the Spartan king. Why did this plan work?

answers.text: It tricked the Spartans into thinking that the Thebans were running away from the field.
It gave the Thebans more men than the Spartans had in total, so the Spartans were surrounded.
It put overwhelming force against the strongest part of the line, and Spartans were not used to losing.
It kept the Sacred Band out of the fighting, so that the best Theban soldiers could be saved.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartans put their best men on their right, twelve rows deep, as was usual. Epaminondas did the opposite and struck exactly where the Spartans were strongest. The lesson calls it a case where a brilliant idea changed history.

questions.text: Why was freeing Messenia such a heavy blow to Sparta?

answers.text: It gave Thebes control of the Spartan fleet, so that Thebes could now rule all of the Aegean.
It forced Sparta to join the Persian king, who then took the Spartans as his own soldiers.
It turned the Spartiates into farmers, who had to work the fields with their own hands.
Sparta lost much of its land and the helots who grew its food, and its power never came back.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartiates were soldiers and the helots grew their food. Without Messenia, Sparta lost much of its land and its workers. The lesson says its power never came back.

questions.text: Xenophon says there was even more confusion in Greece after Mantinea than before. What does this suggest about Thebes's attempt to lead?

answers.text: Thebes ruled Greece peacefully for centuries, and the Greeks never again went to war with it.
Other cities would not accept Thebes as leader, just as they had refused Sparta and Athens.
The Persians took over the leadership of Greece, and the cities paid tribute to the king.
The Greeks agreed that Sparta should lead again, and the Spartans took back all that they had lost.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Thebes thought it should lead Greece, but other cities would not accept it. Epaminondas died at Mantinea, and the lesson ends with the Greeks tired, divided, and without a leader.
