quizzes.title: 26.1 Reading Quiz: Philip II and the Macedonian Machine

questions.text: Philip spent some years as a hostage in Thebes, when Epaminondas was making that city great. What can we reasonably infer about the effect on Philip?

answers.text: He grew to hate all Greek cities, and he swore that he would one day make them pay for it.
He learned nothing there that he later used, since Macedonia fought in its own way.
He decided to give up the throne, and only his brother's death brought him back to Macedonia.
He likely saw how a trained army could beat a larger one, and he later put that idea to use.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Philip saw how a trained army could beat a bigger one, but adds that we cannot be sure what he learned. The inference is a fair one because he went on to rebuild the Macedonian army.

questions.text: Philip's foot soldiers carried the sarissa, a pike more than twelve feet long, and nobles rode beside them as the Companion cavalry. How did the two parts work together?

answers.text: The pike line held the enemy in place, and the cavalry struck at the weak spot or the side.
The cavalry held the enemy in place while the pikes marched up and chased them down the hill.
Both stayed behind the walls of the city while the generals decided where to send them.
The pikemen and horsemen took turns fighting each battle, with one group resting while the other fought.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls the pike line a moving wall that enemies could not easily reach. The pikemen did not have to win alone. They only had to hold the enemy while the cavalry rode around and hit from the side.

questions.text: Philip took the city of Amphipolis and the gold mines near it. Why did that matter so much to his plans?

answers.text: The mines gave Macedonia a famous harbor, which brought in trade from all around the sea.
Greek cities refused to trade with him without it, so he needed the mines to buy grain.
A full-time, paid army was costly, and the gold gave him steady money for wages.
It let him avoid ever using diplomacy, since gold could buy any city that stood in his way.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says such an army cost a lot of money, and that the gold from the mines paid for it. It also says Philip used diplomacy, marriages, and treaties alongside the army.

questions.text: Demosthenes urged Athenian citizens to serve in the army themselves instead of hiring mercenaries. What did he believe?

answers.text: That Athens should make peace with Philip at once, and that the war could never be won.
That freedom must be defended by citizens who are willing to give up comfort, time, and money.
That the Athenian fleet was too small to matter, and that only the Spartans could stop Philip.
That the festivals should be made longer, so that the people could rest from their worries.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Demosthenes was not trying to frighten people for no reason. He thought freedom must be defended by citizens, and he complained that Athenians preferred festivals to war.

questions.text: After Chaeronea, the Greek states kept running their own affairs at home. What had changed for them?

answers.text: They had to give up their gods and worship the king instead.
They no longer had any assemblies at all, and Philip's officers made every law for them.
They became part of Persia, and a satrap was sent to each city to collect the tribute.
They could no longer decide questions of war and peace for themselves.

questions.feedback_general: Philip called the states together at Corinth, and they agreed to keep the peace among themselves and to follow him against Persia. The cities were still there, but they now followed a king.

quizzes.title: 26.2 Reading Quiz: Alexander Invades Persia

questions.text: When Thebes revolted in 335 BC, Alexander destroyed the city. What did the rest of Greece take from this?

answers.text: That Alexander was too busy with other wars to answer any revolt that might be started.
That Athens would soon take Thebes's place as the strongest city in all of central Greece.
That revolt against the new king would be punished harshly, and the revolts stopped.
That Sparta would come to their aid, since the Spartans had always been the enemies of Thebes.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the rest of Greece took the lesson and the revolts stopped. It adds that the act was ruthless and that Alexander could be kind and cruel in the same year.

questions.text: At Issus the armies met on a narrow plain between the mountains and the sea. Why did that help Alexander?

answers.text: The Persians had no horses, so they were forced to fight on foot against the Macedonians.
Darius was not present, so the Persian soldiers lost heart quickly.
The Greeks were fighting at home, and so they knew every hill and stream of the land.
In such a tight space, the Persians could not use their much larger numbers.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Persians could not use their big numbers on a narrow plain. Historians still ask why Darius chose to fight in that place instead of waiting on open ground.

questions.text: After Issus, Alexander did not chase Darius. He went south to take the great port cities. What was his reason?

answers.text: The Persian fleet was crewed by men from those cities, so without them it would have nowhere to land.
He wanted to spend the winter near Athens, where the Greek cities could send him fresh troops.
He had promised the priests of Egypt that he would visit, and he did not wish to break his word.
He was afraid of Darius's army, and he hoped that the sea would keep the Persians from him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that without the ports the Persian fleet had nowhere to go. That is why Tyre mattered, even though it took seven months and a causeway of rubble to win it.

questions.text: Egypt welcomed Alexander. Which of the following helps explain why?

answers.text: Egypt had been a Greek colony for centuries, and many Egyptians already spoke the Greek tongue.
The Egyptians had not liked Persian rule, and Egypt's grain and wealth gave him food and money.
The Egyptians feared that Alexander would burn Memphis, so they gave him the keys to the city.
The Persian king had sent his army there to protect it, and Alexander won the soldiers over.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Egypt had disliked Persian rule and was one of the richest lands in the world. Taking it gave Alexander food, money, and safety for his rear.

questions.text: The lesson says Alexander was brave, quick, and trusted by his men, but also lucky. Which statement best fits that view?

answers.text: His victories were certain from the start, since no army in the world could stand against his own.
Luck alone explains his victories, because he made one careless mistake after another on the field.
Skill and luck worked together, and a few small changes at the Granicus or Issus might have changed it all.
His army was larger than the Persian army in every battle, so the outcome was never in doubt.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that a blow landing a little differently at the Granicus, or a king who waited at Issus, might have changed everything. Historians weigh his skill and the chances of the moment together.

quizzes.title: 27.1 Reading Quiz: The Conqueror and His Limits

questions.text: Ancient writers disagree about why the palace at Persepolis was burned. What should a careful reader take from that?

answers.text: That the fire was certainly an accident, since every writer agrees that no one lit it on purpose.
That a story told in only a few sources, with disagreements among them, should be held with caution.
That Alexander was not present in Persia, and that the army was led by his generals instead.
That Thais should be believed because she was a witness, and her account is the oldest we have.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says we cannot be sure what really happened, and it is wise to keep that in mind whenever a story is told in only a few sources.

questions.text: Alexander put on Persian clothing and took Persian officials into his court. What was a reason for this?

answers.text: He had forgotten his Greek and Macedonian customs after so many years far away from home.
He wanted to leave Persia as soon as possible, and he hoped that the clothing would help him pass.
He planned to give the empire back to Darius's family, and the Persian officials would help him.
He ruled millions of Persians and needed them to accept him, since a king who ruled only by the sword would fear revolts.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he had his reasons: he now ruled millions of Persians and needed them to accept him. The Macedonians, who had followed a king who fought beside them, grew bitter.

questions.text: Alexander asked his companions to bow to him in the Persian custom. Why did this cause trouble?

answers.text: To Persians it was good manners, but to Greeks and Macedonians such bowing was meant for gods.
The Persians saw it as an insult, because their own custom was to stand and to look the king in the eye.
The Macedonians did not know how to bow, and the ceremony became a joke at the king's court.
It was against the law in Persia, and the king could be punished by the priests for asking it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the same act meant different things to different peoples. To Greeks and Macedonians it looked as though their king was behaving like an eastern ruler, and they grew bitter.

questions.text: At the river we call the Beas, the army refused to march farther east. What does this show about leadership?

answers.text: That soldiers should never be given rest on a long march.
That a leader who never loses a battle is never stopped, no matter what his men may think.
That even a great leader needs followers who are willing to go on.
That Porus was stronger than Alexander, and the army had decided that it could not defeat him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the man who had never lost a battle was stopped by his own soldiers, who were worn out after eight years, many wounded, and soaked by the monsoon. Even a great leader needs those who follow.

questions.text: After he killed Cleitus, Alexander is said to have refused to eat for days. What does the lesson draw from this story?

answers.text: That Cleitus had planned to kill him, and Alexander was forced to act in order to save his own life.
That a person with great power who cannot control his temper may do terrible harm and feel horror afterward.
That Alexander wanted to give up the throne, and only the pleading of his soldiers made him change his mind.
That the army approved of the killing, and Alexander only fasted in order to honor the dead man.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls it a warning about what happens when a person with great power cannot control his temper. Cleitus was the officer who had saved Alexander's life at the Granicus.

quizzes.title: 27.2 Reading Quiz: The Hellenistic World

questions.text: Why did Alexander's empire break apart after his death?

answers.text: His heir was only a baby, and no general was strong enough to hold everything together.
The Persian king returned with a new army and took back the empire in a single campaign.
The Greek cities voted to leave the empire, and the generals could not bring them back.
His generals could not find enough soldiers, and so each of them left to raise a new army at home.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Alexander left no grown heir and made no plan for after his death. His generals fought for forty years, and three great kingdoms stood in the end.

questions.text: The word Hellenistic means Greek-like. A farmer in the kingdom of Seleucus would most likely have lived how?

answers.text: As a Greek citizen who spoke only Greek and who voted in the assembly of a free city.
As a slave in the great library at Alexandria, where he copied books for the Ptolemies.
Keeping his own gods, laws, and language, while Greek officials and settlers ran the new cities.
As a soldier in the Macedonian pike line, which marched from one end of the kingdom to the other.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson warns not to imagine one blended world. In Egypt, Syria, and the far east most people were not Greek, and they kept their own gods, laws, and languages. The Greeks ruled and lived in their own cities.

questions.text: Greek became the common language of trade across many lands. What was one effect?

answers.text: No one needed to study Greek anymore, since every merchant had a clerk who spoke for him.
Merchants stopped traveling, because the roads were closed by the soldiers of the new kings.
Every people gave up its own language, and the old tongues of Egypt and Persia soon died out.
A merchant could travel from Egypt to Bactria and do business in Greek, so goods and ideas moved easily.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says this is one reason the Greek language lasted so long. Money, ideas, and goods moved along the roads between the new cities.

questions.text: The Ptolemies built a great library and paid scholars to work in Alexandria. What does this suggest about their aims?

answers.text: They wanted to hide knowledge from other kings, and so they kept every book locked in the palace.
They wanted Alexandria to be the center of Greek learning and had the wealth to pay for it.
They had no interest in books, but they hoped that the scholars would bring them fame.
They wanted to move the scholars to Athens, which was the old home of Greek thought.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a library needed a great deal of money and many workers to copy books by hand. The kings of Egypt wanted Alexandria to be the center of Greek learning, and they spent money to make it so.

questions.text: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, an everyday Egyptian script, and Greek. What does this tell us?

answers.text: That Greek kings ruled Egypt while Egyptian priests still ran the temples and wrote in their own way.
That the Egyptians had forgotten how to write, and the Greek scribes had to teach them again.
That the Greek kings had been driven out of Egypt, and the priests had taken the power back.
That only the Greek writing was important to the priests, who used it for every temple record.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the stone shows Greek kings ruling Egypt while Egyptian priests still ran the temples. The Greek part later helped a scholar read the hieroglyphs for the first time in centuries.

quizzes.title: 27.10 Quarter 3 Exam: Greece from the City-States to Alexander's Heirs
quizzes.description: This exam covers Weeks 19 to 27. It has 36 multiple-choice questions, and each question has one best answer. Read each question slowly and think back to your lessons and primary sources. You have one attempt.

questions.text: The mountains divided the Greeks, but the sea tied them together. Which statement best explains why?

answers.text: Fishing made farming unnecessary, so the Greeks stopped fighting each other for land.
The sea kept foreign traders away from every Greek harbor, so the cities were left alone.
Ships crossed the Aegean faster than farmers crossed mountains, so Greeks became traders.
Greek rulers used the sea to march armies from one city to the next and unite them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says ships crossed the Aegean faster than a farmer could cross mountains. Greeks became sailors and traders and carried their language, gods, and stories wherever they sailed.

questions.text: Hoplites bought their own armor. What does that tell you about who could serve as a hoplite?

answers.text: Men with some wealth could join, so many were farmers and not only nobles.
Only nobles could join, because no one else in the city could pay for the armor.
Only winners of the Olympic Games were allowed to join the phalanx of their city.
Anyone could join, because the armor cost almost nothing to make and buy.

questions.feedback_general: A full set of bronze armor was expensive, but many hoplites were farmers who owned enough land to pay for it. That is why hoplites were not only nobles.

questions.text: What was the main work of the helots in the Spartan lands?

answers.text: They trained Spartan boys in the harsh school called the agoge.
They served as the two kings who led the Spartan army.
They traded iron bars with other cities for goods and food.
They farmed the land and handed over much of every harvest.

questions.feedback_general: The helots were state-owned farm workers. They farmed for the Spartans, which left the Spartiates free to train for war.

questions.text: Each year the Spartan citizens chose five officials who kept watch over everyone, even the kings. What were these officials called?

answers.text: The council of elders (Gerousia).
The overseers (ephors).
The dwellers around (perioikoi).
The full citizens (Spartiates).

questions.feedback_general: The five overseers were the ephors. They watched over everyone, including the two kings, which helped keep any one person from taking all the power.

questions.text: In Athens around 600 BC, why was a bad harvest so dangerous for a small farmer?

answers.text: The nobles took the whole harvest as a tax, whether the crop had failed or not.
A farmer who could not repay a loan could be seized, with his family, as a slave.
The Areopagus sent away any farmer whose crop had failed, and gave his land to nobles.
Farmers who lost a crop were sent to fight in foreign wars to pay off what they owed.

questions.feedback_general: Farmers borrowed from rich neighbors and promised their land. If they still could not pay, the lender could seize the farmer and his family as slaves. That is why the city came close to civil war.

questions.text: Solon sorted Athenians into four classes by wealth. Which class owned a team of oxen and could pay for a hoplite's armor?

answers.text: The horsemen, who served in the cavalry.
The laborers (thetes), who worked for others.
The largest landowners, the five-hundred-measure men.
The middle farmers (zeugitai).

questions.feedback_general: The third class, the zeugitai, were middle farmers. They owned a team of oxen and could afford hoplite armor.

questions.text: Once a year the Athenians could vote to send a powerful man away for ten years. What was this practice meant to prevent?

answers.text: It was meant to stop any one man from growing strong enough to become a tyrant.
It was meant to choose the members of the Council of Five Hundred each year.
It was meant to punish citizens who skipped the Assembly without a good reason.
It was meant to pick the generals who would lead the army in each year's war.

questions.feedback_general: This was ostracism. A man who got the most votes had to leave for ten years, so no one could grow too strong and make himself a tyrant.

questions.text: The lesson says the system of Cleisthenes was not yet a full democracy. Which fact supports that statement?

answers.text: Citizens were not allowed to speak in the Assembly.
The Assembly met only once every ten years.
The old Council of the Hill of Ares still held great power.
Women could vote, but men who were slaves could not.

questions.feedback_general: The old council still held great power. Real change would wait for Ephialtes in 462 BC, and many people were still left out of citizenship.

questions.text: Herodotus says Darius had a servant speak to him at every dinner. What was the servant to say?

answers.text: Master, remember Marathon.
Master, Athens will fall.
Master, send more ships.
Master, remember the Athenians.

questions.feedback_general: When Darius heard that the Athenians had joined the revolt, he shot an arrow into the sky and ordered a servant to say, "Master, remember the Athenians," three times at every dinner.

questions.text: What happened at the sea battle near the island of Lade in 494 BC?

answers.text: Some Ionian ships sailed away without fighting, and the Greek line fell apart.
The Athenian fleet sank the Persian ships and saved the city of Miletus from attack.
A storm wrecked the Persian fleet before it could attack the Ionian ships.
Spartan ships arrived late and joined the Ionians as the battle was ending.

questions.feedback_general: At Lade, some Ionian ships left without fighting and the Greek line fell apart. The Persians won and then destroyed Miletus.

questions.text: Why did the Persians choose the plain of Marathon for their landing?

answers.text: It was next to Sparta, which had promised to help them.
It was protected by tall walls and a deep harbor.
Its flat, open plain suited their horsemen.
No Greek ship could enter the bay.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Persians chose Marathon because its flat, open plain suited their horsemen.

questions.text: At Marathon the Greek center was thin on purpose, and the sides were thick. How did this plan help?

answers.text: It let the strongest men guard the ships on the beach.
When the Persian center pushed through, the Greek sides closed in around it.
It made it easy for the center to retreat.
It let the thick sides reach the Persian ships first.

questions.feedback_general: The Persian center pushed through the thin Greek middle, and the thick Greek sides closed in around it. The Persians broke and ran back to their ships.

questions.text: Why did Xerxes have a canal dug across the neck of the peninsula at Mount Athos?

answers.text: So his ships could avoid the rough sea where an earlier Persian fleet was wrecked.
So he could block the Greek fleet from sailing north and joining the Greek allies.
So his army could bring fresh water down from the mountains to the sea.
So he could mark the border between Persia and Greece for all later kings.

questions.feedback_general: An earlier Persian fleet had been wrecked in the rough sea there. The canal let ships avoid it, one sign that Persia planned carefully to win.

questions.text: How did a Persian force get behind the Greeks at Thermopylae?

answers.text: The Greek allies opened the pass in the night and let the Persians through.
The Persian fleet landed soldiers behind the Greek line on the narrow beach.
A bridge of boats carried the whole army around the mountains by sea.
A local man, Ephialtes, told them about a goat path over the mountains.

questions.feedback_general: Ephialtes, hoping for a reward, told the Persians about a goat path over the mountains. Xerxes sent a force along it at night.

questions.text: The workers at the Laurion mines struck a rich vein of silver. What did Themistocles persuade the Athenians to do with it?

answers.text: Divide it among all the citizens.
Spend it on about two hundred new warships.
Pay the Spartans to join the alliance.
Build a great temple on the Acropolis.

questions.feedback_general: Many Athenians wanted to divide the silver. Themistocles persuaded them to build ships instead, and the fleet later won at Salamis.

questions.text: Who commanded the Greek army that broke the Persian line at Plataea in 479 BC?

answers.text: Themistocles, the Athenian who planned Salamis.
Leonidas, the Spartan king from Thermopylae.
Pausanias, a Spartan commander.
Miltiades, the Athenian general from Marathon.

questions.feedback_general: The Greeks gathered the largest army they had ever raised, and a Spartan commander named Pausanias led it. The Persian general Mardonius was killed.

questions.text: The Delian League kept its treasury on Delos at first. What happened to the treasury around 454 BC?

answers.text: It was moved to Sparta for safekeeping.
It was moved from Athens back to Delos.
It was moved from Delos to Athens.
It was moved to Corinth.

questions.feedback_general: Around 454 BC the treasury was moved from Delos to Athens. The lesson says a league of equals had become an empire.

questions.text: What did Ephialtes do in 462 BC?

answers.text: He took most powers from the Areopagus and gave them to the Assembly and the courts.
He made himself tyrant of Athens and ruled the city for the next ten years.
He led the Greek fleet to victory at Salamis and then became the leader of the city.
He ended the pay for jurors so that only wealthy citizens could serve on juries.

questions.feedback_general: Ephialtes took away most of the powers of the Areopagus and gave them to the Assembly and the people's jury courts. Soon afterward he was killed.

questions.text: In the festival plays of Athens, what was a choregos?

answers.text: A judge, chosen by lot, who awarded the prizes at the festival.
A rich citizen who paid for a chorus as a duty to the city.
A priest who led the procession to the god Dionysus each spring.
A playwright who won the contest and took home a prize.

questions.feedback_general: A choregos paid for the training and costumes of a chorus. If the chorus won, he won glory, and so did the city.

questions.text: Which play is the oldest Greek play we still have, and shows the war from the Persian side?

answers.text: Antigone, by Sophocles.
The Clouds, by Aristophanes.
The Histories, by Herodotus.
The Persians, by Aeschylus.

questions.feedback_general: Aeschylus wrote The Persians in 472 BC, only a few years after Salamis. It is the oldest Greek play we still have.

questions.text: The Athenians blamed Pericles for the war. What happened to him next?

answers.text: He was exiled by the Assembly and never came back to the city of Athens.
He was killed in a battle near Corcyra while leading the Athenian fleet.
He resigned his office and went to live in Sparta for the rest of his life.
They fined him, then chose him again, and he died of illness in 429 BC.

questions.feedback_general: The Athenians fined Pericles, then soon chose him again. He fell ill and died in 429 BC, a heavy loss for Athens.

questions.text: In which quarrel had Athens shut people out of the harbors and markets of its empire, leading them to complain to Sparta?

answers.text: Corcyra
Megara
Potidaea
Melos

questions.feedback_general: Athens shut the people of Megara out of the harbors and markets of its empire. The Megarians carried their complaint to Sparta.

questions.text: After Alcibiades ran away to Sparta, what advice did he give the Spartans?

answers.text: Send a commander to Syracuse and build a fort inside Athenian land to raid all year.
Make peace with Athens at once, because Sparta could not win a long war at sea.
Pull down the Long Walls of Athens before sending any fleet to the harbor of Piraeus.
Attack Persia before Persia could attack Greece and take the Greek cities.

questions.feedback_general: Alcibiades told the Spartans to send a commander to Syracuse and to set up a fort inside Athens' own land. Sparta did both.

questions.text: Sparta had never been a sea power. What finally gave it a fleet strong enough to beat Athens?

answers.text: Athens gave Sparta its old ships as part of a treaty.
The helots built ships and rowed them for their masters.
Persian money paid for ships and crews.
A storm destroyed the fleet of Athens.

questions.feedback_general: After Sicily, the Persian governor offered Sparta money for ships. With Persian gold Sparta built a fleet, and the money gave it what it had always lacked.

questions.text: After the Thirty fell, the Athenians passed an amnesty. What did the citizens swear?

answers.text: Not to punish each other for what was done during the war and the tyranny.
To send all of the Thirty into exile and take away their land.
To rebuild the Long Walls at once and call back the Athenian fleet.
To end the war by paying tribute to Sparta every year for ten years.

questions.feedback_general: The amnesty was meant to heal the city. It also meant no one could be tried for acts during the tyranny, which may explain the religious charge against Socrates.

questions.text: How did Socrates die?

answers.text: He died as a hoplite in battle while defending the city from Sparta.
He was killed by the Thirty Tyrants after he refused to follow their orders.
He drank poison after he refused his friends' offer to help him escape.
He died in exile far from Athens after the jury sent him away.

questions.feedback_general: The jury voted for death. Friends offered to help him escape, but Socrates refused and drank the poison hemlock.

questions.text: At Leuctra, where did Epaminondas place his best men?

answers.text: On his right, twelve rows deep, facing the Spartan allies.
On his left, fifty rows deep, aimed straight at the Spartan king.
In the center, in a thin line behind the Sacred Band.
Behind the army, as a guard for the baggage.

questions.feedback_general: Epaminondas did the opposite of what Spartans expected. He packed his best men fifty rows deep on his left and aimed them at the Spartan king and his Spartiates.

questions.text: What did Epaminondas do when he marched into Messenia?

answers.text: He made Messenia a province of Thebes and sent Theban governors there.
He burned the Messenian farms to starve Sparta into surrender.
He gave the land back to the Spartans in return for a long peace.
He set the helots free and helped them build a walled city.

questions.feedback_general: Epaminondas freed the Messenians and helped them build a walled city. Sparta lost much of its land and its workers, and its power never came back.

questions.text: What happened at Chaeronea in 338 BC?

answers.text: Athens and Thebes beat Philip and drove his army out of Greece for many years to come.
Philip beat Athens and Thebes, and the Sacred Band was killed almost to the last man.
Sparta joined Philip and helped him destroy the city of Athens.
Philip was killed there by one of his own bodyguards at a royal wedding.

questions.feedback_general: Philip and Alexander won at Chaeronea. After the battle, Philip treated Athens gently but put a garrison in Thebes. Philip was killed two years later, not at Chaeronea.

questions.text: What did the Greek states agree to when Philip called them together at Corinth?

answers.text: To keep the peace among themselves and follow Philip in a war against Persia.
To make Philip the king of Athens and give him the Athenian fleet.
To pay tribute to the king of Persia in return for a lasting peace.
To destroy the city of Thebes and divide its land among the other states.

questions.feedback_general: The states agreed to keep the peace among themselves and follow Philip against Persia. Only Sparta refused.

questions.text: What did Alexander do about the island city of Tyre?

answers.text: He made peace with its leaders and moved on to Egypt without a fight.
He sailed past it with the Persian fleet and attacked the mainland instead.
He left it alone and marched straight to Egypt, because its walls were too high to take.
He built a causeway of rubble out to the island, and it fell after seven months.

questions.feedback_general: Tyre was an island city with high walls. Alexander built a causeway out to it, which took seven months, and the city fell in 332 BC.

questions.text: Parmenion is said to have advised a night attack before the big battle on the plain. What did Alexander answer?

answers.text: That the moon was too bright.
That his soldiers were too tired.
That he would not steal a victory.
That Darius had asked for a truce.

questions.feedback_general: The story goes that Alexander answered that he would not steal a victory. The next day he led his horsemen in a wedge toward Darius.

questions.text: Why did the army stop at the river we call the Beas?

answers.text: The soldiers were worn out and homesick after eight years, and they refused to go on.
King Porus had blocked the river with his elephants and Alexander could not cross.
Alexander had fallen ill with a fever and could no longer lead the army.
A new Persian army had arrived from the west and cut off the way home.

questions.feedback_general: In a mutiny, the soldiers said they would go no farther. Alexander sulked for three days and then turned back. Even a great leader needs followers.

questions.text: What happened to Darius III after he fled to the east?

answers.text: He gave himself up to Alexander and was treated as a guest of honor.
He was crowned a god in Bactria and ruled there for many years.
He escaped to India and lived there under the protection of King Porus.
His own nobles, led by Bessus, seized and killed him.

questions.feedback_general: Bessus, the governor of Bactria, led the nobles who killed Darius in 330 BC. Alexander buried him with royal honors and hunted Bessus down.

questions.text: Eratosthenes noticed that a well in southern Egypt had no shadow at noon while a stick in Alexandria did. What did he work out from this?

answers.text: When the Nile would flood.
How tall the Pharos was.
How big the Earth is.
Where the sun god lived.

questions.feedback_general: From the difference in shadows and the distance between the cities, he worked out the size of the Earth. His answer was remarkably close to the real one.

questions.text: Some of the edicts of King Asoka were written in Greek. What does this show?

answers.text: He had been born in Macedonia and had learned to write Greek as a boy.
Greeks lived in his kingdom, and Greek was common enough for an Indian king to use.
Alexander had ordered the edicts to be carved on every rock and pillar.
Greek was the only written language in India at the time of Asoka.

questions.feedback_general: A few edicts were written in Greek for the Greeks living in his kingdom. The Greek language had become so common that even an Indian king used it.

questions.text:

Before you begin the lessons, write your first answer in two or three sentences. A guess is fine. You will answer the same question again at the end of the module.

By the end of this module you should be able to:

  • Describe the land around Rome and why it helped the city grow.
  • Tell the story of how Rome became a republic.
  • Explain the difference between patricians and plebeians.
  • Explain why the Twelve Tables mattered.
  • Name the main Roman offices and what each one did.
  • Explain how the Senate, the people, and the tribunes checked each other.
  • Describe how Polybius judged the Roman government.

Have you read these goals?

I read them, but I have a question for my teacher.

quizzes.title: 28.1 Reading Quiz: From Romulus to the Republic

questions.text: The Romans told stories about Aeneas and about Romulus and Remus, and Livy wrote them down about seven hundred years after the events. What should a careful reader conclude about these stories?

answers.text: They are exact history, because Livy was a Roman who knew his own city and its oldest records well.
They show what the Romans believed about themselves, even if we cannot be sure they are exact history.
They are false, so they teach us nothing at all about the Romans or about how they saw their past.
They were written down at the time of Romulus, and Livy only copied them out again for his readers.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says we cannot be sure how much is true. Diggers found huts from about that time, so a village really existed, but Livy used old stories passed from person to person. The tales still show that the Romans saw themselves as tough, loyal, and proud.

questions.text: After the king fled in 509 BC, the Romans did not choose a new king. They chose two consuls who each served for one year. What does this choice suggest?

answers.text: They wanted a faster way to fight their wars, since one king could not lead two armies at once.
They had no one in the city who could lead, so they let two men take turns at the work.
They hoped the Etruscans would soon return, and two consuls could greet the king when he came.
They feared one man holding power for long, so they split power and limited the time.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Rome could have kept a king, as other Italian cities did. Choosing two officials with short terms shows that the Romans no longer trusted any one man with lasting power.

questions.text: In 494 BC the plebeians marched out of the city and refused to fight or work. Why did the patricians have to listen?

answers.text: Rome needed the plebeians' labor and their spears.
The plebeians had taken over the Senate, and they now held all of the offices in the city.
The Etruscans had joined the plebeians against Rome.
The patricians had already agreed to give up their offices.

questions.feedback_general: The plebeians were the great majority. They were farmers, craftsmen, and shopkeepers, and they fought in the army. Without them Rome could not work or fight, so the two sides agreed that the plebeians could choose tribunes.

questions.text: Historians who admire the Roman Republic often point to the Conflict of the Orders as a source of Roman strength. What about it do they admire?

answers.text: It ended quickly after one great battle, won by the plebeians.
The plebeians won every right they wanted at once, and the patricians gave no more trouble.
Both sides bargained and gave something up, so it never became a civil war.
The patricians kept all the power, and the plebeians stopped asking for any change in the laws.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the struggle lasted about two hundred years and that patricians gave way a little at a time. Because both sides bargained, Rome avoided civil war. This habit of compromise is what admirers praise.

questions.text: The Twelve Tables were sometimes harsh. Why did the lesson still call their greatest value so important?

answers.text: They made sure only patrician judges knew the law, so that disputes were settled by the old families.
Everyone could now read the laws, which made it harder for a powerful person to twist them.
They ended debt and slavery in Rome, so that no citizen could ever be sold for what he owed.
They gave plebeians the right to be consul at once, and the old families lost their offices.

questions.feedback_general: The plebeians had complained that the laws were secret and that patrician judges could bend them. Once the laws were written and displayed in the Forum, they bound everyone. The lesson calls this idea the rule of law.

quizzes.title: 28.2 Reading Quiz: Consuls, Senate, and People

questions.text: Each consul could stop the other, and a consul had to step down after a year. What problem were the Romans trying to solve?

answers.text: Too few men were willing to take office.
The high cost of paying officials.
The danger of one man holding power like a king.
The need to make decisions more quickly in war.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans feared that one man with too much power would act like a king. So they set short terms, split the work among many hands, and let each consul check the other.

questions.text: The Senate could not pass laws by itself, but its advice carried great weight. What helps explain this?

answers.text: Senators served for life and so knew more about government than any one-year consul.
Senators commanded the army, and so the consuls had to follow their orders in every war.
Senators were chosen by lot every year, and so every citizen had a turn to give advice.
Senators could remove the tribunes, and so no one dared to ignore what the Senate wished.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says most senators were former officials, and they served for life. A consul stayed in office only a year, so he leaned on the Senate's experience.

questions.text: A dictator held full power, but only for six months. Why did the Romans trust such an office?

answers.text: The consuls watched over every decision a dictator made, and could overrule him at any time.
Dictators were always young men with no army of their own.
The Senate named a dictator only in times of peace, when there was no danger to the city.
They believed good men would give up power when the danger passed.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans trusted this office because they believed good men would give up power once the emergency was over. It sets up next week's story of a man who did exactly that.

questions.text: Polybius thought Rome's government blended kingly, aristocratic, and democratic parts. Why did he think this mixture made Rome stable?

answers.text: It let the strongest part rule without any check, so that the city could always act quickly.
Each part could check the others and needed the others to get anything done.
It copied the government of Athens exactly, with all its strengths.
It gave all the power to the common people, who could then choose any law that they liked.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each part could check the others and each needed the others. Polybius believed this mixture gave Rome more stability than any one kind of government alone.

questions.text: A Roman farmer could vote, serve as a soldier, and perhaps one day be elected. Even so, the lesson says the share of people who truly ruled was smaller than the whole population. Why?

answers.text: Only patricians were allowed to vote, and a farmer had to ask a patrician to speak for him.
Farmers were not allowed to take part in the assemblies, since they lived too far from the city.
Rome had no assemblies, so the consuls made every choice.
Women, children, slaves, and many foreigners could not vote or hold office.

questions.feedback_general: Only free adult men who were citizens could both vote and hold office. Born citizens who were women had some legal rights but no vote. Slaves had no rights. As in Athens, the ruling group was smaller than the population.

quizzes.title: 29.1 Reading Quiz: The Legion and the Conquest of Italy

questions.text: Roman soldiers were citizens who owned land and bought their own weapons. Why did that make them fight so hard?

answers.text: A lost battle might cost a farmer his own home, so he had every reason to win.
They were paid higher wages than any hired soldier in the world.
The law forced them to fight all year long.
They hoped that each victory would make them dictator.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that because they fought for their own farms, they fought hard. A farmer who lost a battle might lose his home.

questions.text: About 390 BC the Gauls burned much of Rome. What did the Romans do afterward, and what does it show?

answers.text: They gave up the city and moved away to a safer place.
They made peace with the Gauls and stopped training their soldiers, since the war was over.
They rebuilt, put up strong walls, and trained harder.
They asked the Etruscans to rule them, hoping that a strong king would keep the Gauls away.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the disaster could have been the end of the city, but the Romans rebuilt, put up strong walls, and trained harder. It shows a stubbornness that Rome would need again.

questions.text: A legion was split into maniples that stood in rows with gaps, like the squares on a checkerboard. Why did this help on rough ground?

answers.text: Soldiers in a legion carried much longer spears, which could reach over the rough ground.
Each maniple could move on its own, and the next line could step forward if one was pushed back.
A legion was so small that it could hide among the trees and rocks and surprise the enemy.
A legion only fought on flat, open plains, so it could always avoid the rough ground.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a maniple could move on its own, so a legion could handle rough ground better than a tight phalanx. If one line was pushed back, the next stepped forward.

questions.text: After a victory, Rome often made the losers allies and asked for soldiers instead of tribute. Why was this a smart choice?

answers.text: It made the allies rich enough to rebel, since they kept all of their tribute for themselves.
It gave Rome gold to spend on a navy, since the allies paid for ships and sailors.
It let Rome avoid all further wars, since the allies were too weak to fight any longer.
Each victory made Rome's army larger, and the allies had something to lose if Rome fell.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each victory made Rome's army larger. Allies kept their lands, laws, and pride, so even defeated enemies had a reason to stay loyal.

questions.text: Pyrrhus beat the Romans in two battles, yet he went home in 275 BC. What explains this?

answers.text: The Romans had more elephants than he did, and the elephants won the third battle.
His elephants refused to fight a third time, and his soldiers would not march without them.
Rome could raise more troops from its allies, but he could not replace his lost men.
The Greek cities of the south joined Rome before the first battle, and he was cut off from home.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each win cost him many of his best men. Rome kept raising troops from its allies, and he could not. That is why a win that costs too much is called a Pyrrhic victory.

quizzes.title: 29.2 Reading Quiz: Rome and Carthage, the First Punic War

questions.text: Most of Carthage's troops were mercenaries. Why might that be a weakness compared with Rome's army?

answers.text: Mercenaries were never given weapons.
They were always badly trained.
Carthaginians would not let them fight at sea.
They fought well when paid, but had less reason to die for the city.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says they fought well when paid but had less reason to die for Carthage. Roman citizen-soldiers were fighting for their own homes.

questions.text: Rome had a big land army but almost no ships, and many observers would have bet on Carthage. Yet Rome voted to help at Messana. What does this suggest about the Romans?

answers.text: The Senate was united and sure of an easy win, since Carthage was far away across the sea.
They were willing to risk a war they were not ready for, and they hated to give up.
Carthage had promised to give Rome the island, and the Romans only wished to take it.
Rome already had the largest navy in the Mediterranean, and it was eager to put it to use.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Senate argued, because the war would be against Carthage, and that the Romans were stubborn and did not like to give up.

questions.text: The raven, or corvus, let Roman soldiers fight on an enemy deck as if on land. Why was this a good fit for Rome?

answers.text: Roman crews lacked skill at handling ships but were strong at close fighting on solid ground.
The raven made Roman ships faster than Carthaginian ships, so they could catch the enemy.
The raven let Roman ships stay far away from the enemy and strike with spears from a distance.
The raven made it unnecessary to build a navy, since Roman soldiers could fight from the shore.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans lacked skill at ships, so they fitted a boarding bridge with a spike and used what they knew best. At Mylae in 260 BC this trick won the first Roman naval victory.

questions.text: Rome lost more ships to storms than to Carthage, and its treasury ran dry. What made a last fleet possible?

answers.text: A loan from Carthage, which hoped to keep Rome from building any more ships.
A new tax on Sicily, paid in silver and in grain.
Rich Romans lent their own money, to be repaid only if Rome won.
Silver brought from Spain, where the Romans had taken the mines away from the Carthaginians.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says rich citizens lent money of their own to build another fleet, with a reward only if Rome won. That fleet crushed the Carthaginians at the Aegates Islands in 241 BC.

questions.text: Polybius himself thought one Roman act after the war was unjust. Which act was it?

answers.text: Seizing Sardinia and Corsica while Carthage was too weak to resist.
Making Sicily a Roman province.
Asking Carthage to pay a large sum over many years.
Sending Regulus to Africa.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Rome took Sardinia and Corsica while Carthage was fighting its own mercenaries, though Rome had no good reason. Hamilcar Barca came home angry, and his young son Hannibal was watching.

quizzes.title: 30.1 Reading Quiz: Hannibal Crosses the Alps

questions.text: Hannibal ate what his soldiers ate and slept on the ground in his cloak. What does this suggest about why his army followed him?

answers.text: He was a rich man who paid them better than anyone else.
Their laws forced them to obey any general, and no soldier had ever refused an order before.
He shared their hardships, so they loved and trusted him.
He kept them from learning how dangerous the march would be.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the soldiers loved him and that he ate what they ate and slept on the ground. A leader who shares hardship earns loyalty that money cannot buy.

questions.text: Rome ruled the sea, so Hannibal could not sail an army to Italy. What did that force him to do?

answers.text: March his army by land through Gaul and across the Alps.
Wait in Spain until the Romans attacked.
Ask Carthage to send a second fleet.
Make peace with Rome before the war began.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he decided to march, over the Pyrenees, through Gaul, across the Rhone, and over the Alps in late autumn.

questions.text: Polybius says Hannibal reached Italy with only about twenty thousand foot soldiers and six thousand horsemen, out of a much larger army. What can we infer?

answers.text: The Romans had destroyed part of his army earlier, and he had been forced to make up the loss.
Hannibal sent most of his men home on purpose, because he thought a small army would move faster.
The march was very costly, so he could not hope to win by numbers alone.
The Alps were easy to cross, and the army lost few men.

questions.feedback_general: Some men were left to guard Spain, but many were lost on the march. The lesson says Hannibal knew he could not match Rome in numbers and had to use his wits.

questions.text: At Cannae the Romans put their strongest troops in the center and planned to push straight through. How did Hannibal use that plan against them?

answers.text: He ran away and left the field, so that the Romans thought that they had already won the day.
He put his best men in the center to block them, and the Romans were stopped at the first charge.
He used elephants to break the Roman center, and the soldiers behind them were trampled in the rush.
He let his weaker center bend back while his strong sides and cavalry closed around the Romans.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans were drawn into a pocket and then surrounded, packed so tightly that their numbers meant nothing. This is called a double envelopment.

questions.text: After Cannae, Maharbal said Hannibal knew how to win a victory but not how to use one. What reasons does the lesson give for doubting that Hannibal could simply have taken Rome?

answers.text: Rome had already made peace, and the Senate had sent gifts to Hannibal's camp in the south.
He had no siege machines, Rome had strong walls, and his small army was far from home.
His elephants were too weak to move, and the winter in the mountains had killed most of them.
Carthage had sent a second army to take his place, and the new general refused to attack Rome.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson lists these reasons, and adds that Hannibal needed help from Carthage that never came. It says historians still argue about it and that we cannot know the answer.

quizzes.title: 30.2 Reading Quiz: Fabius, Scipio, and Zama

questions.text: Fabius followed Hannibal at a safe distance and avoided a big fight, and many Romans hated this plan. Why did they later see he had been right?

answers.text: He beat Hannibal quickly, and the Romans saw he was right.
Hannibal could win any open fight, so Rome needed to deny him one.
His term as dictator had ended, and the people saw that the new consuls were no better.
Hannibal ran out of elephants, and the Romans saw that the delay had worn down his army.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that after Cannae the Romans saw that Hannibal could win any open fight. Delay bought Rome the time it needed.

questions.text: Hannibal hoped that Rome's allies would leave it after his big wins, but most stayed loyal. What helps explain this?

answers.text: Hannibal's army treated their lands very gently, but the allies still did not join him.
They feared Roman punishment more than anything else, and the legions were camped in their towns.
Rome paid them large sums each year, and they did not want to lose the money.
They had long been partners of Rome, keeping their own governments and sharing in its spoils.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that for two hundred years Rome had treated its allies as partners. Hannibal was a foreign general with a small army far from home. This is the payoff of the system studied in the week before.

questions.text: Scipio was about twenty-five when the people sent him to Spain, though he held no high office. What does this tell us about Rome in that crisis?

answers.text: Romans were willing to bend their usual rules to put a gifted man in command.
Rome always chose its youngest men as generals, since old men were thought to be too slow.
Rome had no other commanders left alive, and so the people had no one else to send.
The Senate chose him because he was a priest, and a priest could speak to the gods for the army.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls it an unusual choice. His father and uncle had been killed in Spain, and the crisis made Romans willing to set the usual path aside.

questions.text: Hannibal would not leave Italy, so Scipio landed his army in North Africa. Why was this a good answer?

answers.text: It forced Carthage to call Hannibal home to defend the city.
It let Scipio capture Hannibal's army in Italy.
It stopped Carthage from trading with Spain.
It gave Rome a chance to rest its soldiers.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Carthage panicked and called Hannibal home, and the two armies met at Zama in 202 BC. Some senators, including Fabius, thought the plan too risky.

questions.text: Both Hannibal and Scipio ended their lives in bitterness or exile. What does the lesson suggest about the Republic?

answers.text: The Senate always rewarded success, and so the generals of Rome lived out their lives in comfort at home.
Carthage's government was stronger than Rome's, and it kept its generals loyal to the end of their days.
Exile is the usual end for good generals, and Rome treated every general in this way.
A man who won too much glory could become a threat, and the old habit of sharing power needed leaders who stayed among equals.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson ends with this warning. Rivals envied Scipio and accused him of taking bribes. It says the Republic would struggle with this problem over the next century.

quizzes.title: 31.1 Reading Quiz: Carthage Destroyed, Greece Conquered

questions.text: Many historians doubt that Carthage was a danger in 149 BC, yet Rome destroyed it. What does the lesson suggest explains Rome's act?

answers.text: Fear and pride, since Romans had not forgotten Hannibal.
Carthage had attacked Rome first.
Carthage had built a new war fleet.
Carthage had refused to pay anything for fifty years.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Carthage had given up its empire, its navy, and its army, and it was no threat. Fear and pride pushed Rome to a cruel act, and some Romans felt uneasy about it.

questions.text: After 146 BC, many Romans admired Greek learning and copied Greek buildings. How had the Greeks' own situation changed?

answers.text: They taught Roman governors how to rule, and the Greeks gave advice in the Senate itself.
They became equal citizens of Rome, with the same right to vote and to hold office in the city.
They kept their full independence, and Rome only asked them to pay a small yearly gift.
They answered to a Roman governor, and the freedom of the city-states was finished.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Greece was now part of the Roman world. Admiration did not give Greek cities their freedom back.

questions.text: Wars now lasted for years across the sea. Why did that ruin many Roman farmers?

answers.text: Farmers were forbidden to own land, and so they had to work for the nobles and give up their farms.
A farmer away at war for years saw his farm fail, and many had to sell their land.
Slaves took the farmers' places in the army, and the farmers lost their pay and their land.
The Senate taxed farms out of existence, and the farmers could no longer pay for seed.

questions.feedback_general: The citizen-soldier used to serve for a season and go home. Now he might be away a long time, and Hannibal's army had also burned fields in Italy.

questions.text: Rich Romans bought up land and built great estates worked by slaves. Why could a free farmer not compete?

answers.text: Slaves were taught better farming than free men, and so they grew bigger crops on the same land.
Free farmers refused to sell their grain, and so the buyers turned to the great estates instead.
Slaves were cheap and could work all year, while a farmer had only his own two hands.
The Senate banned free farmers from the markets, and so they could not sell what they grew.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says slaves were captured in the wars and cost little. Many families lost their farms and drifted to Rome, where there was little work.

questions.text: Tiberius Gracchus had a rival tribune removed from office, which broke a custom. What was the effect?

answers.text: It made the Senate love him, since the senators had long wished to see the tribune removed.
It ended the quarrel between rich and poor, and the land law was passed with no more trouble.
It made the veto stronger, so no tribune dared to block the people.
It made his enemies fear him more, and violence soon entered Roman politics.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that breaking the custom made his enemies fear him more, and that he was later clubbed to death. It was the first time in generations that Romans had killed each other over politics.

quizzes.title: 31.2 Reading Quiz: Marius and the Army of the Poor

questions.text: Jugurtha bribed senators, and Sallust says he called Rome a city for sale. Why did ordinary Romans grow furious?

answers.text: Jugurtha refused to pay tribute to Rome, and the Roman people felt that he had insulted them.
Senators refused to go to Numidia, and so the Roman people felt that they had been left alone.
Their sons were dying in wars while nobles were taking bribes.
Marius himself had taken a bribe from Jugurtha.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the war dragged on while generals made deals with Jugurtha or failed to win. People began to ask for someone who would not take bribes.

questions.text: Marius was a new man from the small town of Arpinum who said openly that the nobles were weak. Why did the voters turn to him?

answers.text: He was a rich nobleman.
He did not come from the old noble families and had won fame as a soldier.
He was the choice of the Senate.
He had already ended the war in Numidia.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he came from outside the noble families and had a soldier's fame. In 107 BC the voters made him consul, and he brought the war to an end.

questions.text: Marius let poor men without property join the army. Why was this both smart and dangerous?

answers.text: It lowered the pay of every soldier, and so the old soldiers began to leave the army.
It made the Senate stronger, since the poor men now owed their pay and their land to senators.
It forced the Senate to give every soldier land, and so the nobles lost their great estates.
It gave Rome plenty of soldiers, but landless soldiers looked to their general for pay and a future.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a soldier with no land had nothing to go back to, and the Senate often refused him land. The only person who could help him was his general.

questions.text: Marius was elected consul five years in a row, though custom said a man should wait ten years. What does the lesson draw from this?

answers.text: Rome could survive danger only by breaking its own rules, and each emergency gave one man more power.
Marius had cheated in every election, and the voters did not find out until much later.
The Senate had given up its power on purpose, hoping that one man could save the Republic.
Roman custom had no force at all, and no one in the city had ever followed it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that danger had become a habit. Each emergency gave one man more power.

questions.text: In 88 BC Sulla led his army to the gates of Rome and entered the city. What did this show?

answers.text: That Roman soldiers never obeyed a general, and so Sulla had to take the city by himself.
That a general with loyal legions could seize the city, and the laws could not stop him.
That the Social War was over, and the soldiers were now free to go back to their homes.
That the Senate had asked him to defend the city, and the consuls opened the gates for him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says no Roman general had ever done this before. Sulla later became dictator with no six-month limit, and he showed that the laws could not stop a general with loyal legions.

quizzes.title: 32.1 Reading Quiz: Spartacus, Pompey, and the First Triumvirate

questions.text: Spartacus began with about seventy runaways, and his army grew to tens of thousands. What can we infer about slavery in Italy?

answers.text: Few slaves wished to be free, and most of the runaways soon went back to their masters.
Slaves were treated kindly on the estates, and so they had no reason to join the revolt.
Slaves were never allowed to fight, and so the runaways had to learn from their captors.
There were many slaves, often captured in Rome's wars, ready to join anyone who broke free.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Italy held hundreds of thousands of slaves by the 70s BC and that slaves from farms and estates flocked to the rebels.

questions.text: The sources disagree about what Spartacus wanted. What should a careful reader do?

answers.text: Say that we cannot be certain, and weigh the accounts instead of choosing the one that sounds best.
Choose the account that makes him a hero, since the Romans who wrote about him were his enemies.
Ignore the revolt, since no one knows what he wanted and the sources cannot be trusted at all.
Trust whatever Crassus said about him, since Crassus was the general who defeated him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson gives two accounts. In one he hoped to lead his people out of Italy over the Alps. In the other the runaways wished to stay and plunder. It says we do not know for certain.

questions.text: After the revolt, about six thousand captured slaves were nailed to crosses along the road from Capua to Rome. What was the purpose?

answers.text: To honor the dead.
To mark the road for travelers.
To serve as a warning, though cruelty made the fear greater.
To pay the soldiers of Crassus.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the crosses were meant as a warning. It adds that cruelty made the fear greater and that no one in the Senate could see a way to end it.

questions.text: Pompey was made consul in 70 BC though he was too young and had not held the lower offices. What does this show?

answers.text: Romans had never cared about age, and there were many young men who held the highest offices.
Romans were willing to bend the rules for a successful general, and such a man might not go back to being an ordinary citizen.
The Senate no longer met, and so the people could choose any man they liked as consul.
Pompey had been a tribune for many years, and so he knew the work of the lower offices.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Senate began to fear him. The old rule was that a general gave up his command when a war ended, and Pompey, like Sulla, made many Romans wonder whether that rule still held.

questions.text: The First Triumvirate was a private pact among Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus. Why did it matter?

answers.text: Real decisions were now made in private by three men, and the Senate was bypassed.
It was an official office that replaced the consuls, and it was voted on by the Assembly.
It ended the quarrels between the three men, and the city enjoyed a long and quiet peace.
It gave the plebeians a new tribune, and the three men agreed to let him speak for them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Republic's offices still existed, but the real decisions were made by three men in a secret deal. Each needed the other two, and none could be sure the pact would last.

quizzes.title: 32.2 Reading Quiz: Caesar in Gaul

questions.text: After his year as consul, Caesar had huge debts and needed a province. Why was Gaul a good choice for him?

answers.text: The Senate forced him to go there.
A war there could win him glory, wealth to pay his debts, and an army loyal to him.
Gaul was already at peace and easy to govern.
Pompey ordered him to go.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a governor had an army, a chance for glory, and a way to get rich. Caesar saw how Sulla and Pompey rose, and he meant to do the same.

questions.text: Caesar built a bridge across the Rhine in ten days and landed in Britain, though these brought little. Why did he bother?

answers.text: To conquer Germany, which he hoped to add to the lands of Rome in a single campaign.
To find gold, which the Romans believed lay in the rivers beyond the Rhine and in Britain.
Because Rome loved a daring story, and each bold deed made him more famous at home.
Because the Senate demanded it, and Caesar had to show that he was obeying its orders.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar knew that Rome loved a daring story, and that such deeds made him famous where his rivals could not match him.

questions.text: Caesar wrote the Commentaries in the third person and called himself Caesar. How should a careful reader take them?

answers.text: As a source with a point of view, since he was a politician who needed support at home.
As a neutral report with no point of view, since he wrote it as plainly as a soldier would.
As proof that everything he said was false, since a man who praises himself cannot be trusted.
As a book written by someone else, since no Roman would write about himself in that way.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the third person makes the book sound as if a neutral reporter were describing the facts. But Caesar made himself look wise, brave, and just. This does not mean he lied all the time, only that we should ask what he wanted Romans to believe.

questions.text: At Alesia, Caesar built one wall facing inward and a second wall facing outward. Why?

answers.text: To keep his own soldiers from deserting, since the siege had lasted through a hard winter.
To keep out the Parthians, who were said to be marching west to help the Gauls.
To hold prisoners for his victory parade, which he planned to hold in Rome that year.
To keep Vercingetorix's army inside and to guard against the Gallic army coming to rescue it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar was trapped between two armies, and that after days of hard fighting the Romans held.

questions.text: Julia died and Crassus was killed at Carrhae. What happened to the triumvirate?

answers.text: Caesar and Pompey became closer friends, and the two men shared the rule of Rome.
Pompey moved to Gaul, where he joined Caesar's army and fought in the last wars.
Two of the ties that held it together were gone, and Pompey and Caesar began to look at each other with suspicion.
The Senate made it an official office, and the two men that were left became its consuls.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says only Pompey and Caesar remained. Pompey stayed near Rome with the Senate leaning toward him, and Caesar was far away with an army.

quizzes.title: 33.1 Reading Quiz: Crossing the Rubicon

questions.text: Caesar asked to run for consul while still in Gaul with his army, and the Senate said no. Why did that refusal worry him so much?

answers.text: He would have to pay a large fine to the Senate for every year that he had held his command in Gaul.
Pompey would take over his province at once, and the army that he had led in Gaul would be taken from him.
Once his command ended he would be a private man, and his enemies could take him to court and ruin him.
He would be forbidden to enter Italy for ten years, and all of his lands in Rome would be taken.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar needed to come home and run for consul again, but as soon as his command ended his enemies could take him to court for what he had done as consul. A man in court could be ruined, even exiled.

questions.text: The lesson says each side thought the other was the aggressor, and that neither would give way. What does this suggest about the coming of the war?

answers.text: Both sides could have stepped back, and neither did, so each helped bring the war on.
Only the Senate wanted a war, and Caesar had tried every means to keep the peace in the end.
Caesar had planned the war for years and no one could stop him, since his army was far too strong.
Nothing anyone did could have prevented it, because the two men had become enemies long before.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Senate could have let Caesar run for consul and the war might have been avoided, and that Caesar could have turned back. It says the Republic died because Roman leaders had spent years refusing to trust one another.

questions.text: Caesar says he was defending his honor and the tribunes' rights, while Plutarch makes the crossing a dramatic gamble. Why might their stories differ?

answers.text: Plutarch was at the river and Caesar was not, so Plutarch had the better view of the crossing.
Caesar never wrote about the war, so Plutarch told it alone.
Both wrote at the same time for the same readers, and so their accounts ought to have been the same.
Each writer shaped the story to what he wanted readers to feel.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each version is shaped by what the writer wanted readers to feel. Caesar wrote about his own war, and Plutarch wrote about 150 years later.

questions.text: At Pharsalus Pompey had far more men, yet he lost. What does the lesson give as part of the reason?

answers.text: Pompey had no horsemen at all, and so his army could not guard its sides against the enemy.
Caesar's veterans had fought together for years and held steady, and a hidden line of foot soldiers turned back the horsemen.
Caesar had a much larger fleet, and it cut Pompey's army off from the grain that it needed.
The Senate refused to send Pompey supplies, and his army was weak from hunger on the day of the battle.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Pompey's horsemen charged and were turned back by a hidden line, and then his army broke and ran. Steady, experienced soldiers mattered more than numbers on paper.

questions.text: Caesar pardoned many of his captured enemies, but Cato refused any pardon and later took his own life. What might Cato's choice show?

answers.text: Cato wanted to become Caesar's friend, but he feared that the other senators would turn against him.
Pardons were never offered in Roman wars, and Cato knew that Caesar would put him to death in the end.
He thought that accepting mercy from Caesar meant accepting that Caesar had the right to rule him, and he would not.
He was afraid of dying in battle, and so he chose to end his own life before the fighting began.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Cato was the strictest senator and kept fighting rather than accept a pardon, and that he took his own life rather than live under Caesar. For him, mercy from one man was a sign that the Republic's rules no longer held.

quizzes.title: 33.2 Reading Quiz: Dictator for Life and the Ides of March

questions.text: The Senate gave Caesar statues, a golden chair, and a purple robe, and then named him dictator for life. Why did these honors alarm old Romans?

answers.text: They cost the Senate too much money, and the treasury was already weak after the years of civil war.
The honors were meant for gods and not for men, and the old Romans feared that Caesar would claim to be a god.
Caesar had refused all honors until then, so Romans wondered why.
Each new honor made Caesar look less like a fellow citizen and more like a ruler.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each new honor made Caesar look less like a fellow citizen and more like a ruler. Rome's old dictators served only six months, but a dictator for life had no limit.

questions.text: At the Wolf Festival Antony offered Caesar a crown, and Caesar pushed it away twice. What is the best reading of this scene?

answers.text: It proves that Caesar wanted to be king, since he would not have taken the crown from Antony's hand in public.
We cannot be sure what it meant, but Romans who remembered the old kings would have felt uneasy either way.
It proves that it was only a joke, because Antony and Caesar had planned the scene as a piece of play.
It shows that Antony wanted to be king himself, and that Caesar only turned the crown away to stop him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says ancient writers could not agree whether it was a test of the crowd or a show planned in advance. It adds that to many senators a ruler who could not be removed was a king in all but name.

questions.text: Brutus had been forgiven by Caesar, yet he joined the plot. What reason does the lesson give?

answers.text: He believed that if one man could grant or take away life at will, Romans were no longer free citizens.
He wanted to become dictator himself, and he thought that the plot was his best way to take the office.
He thought that mercy was a sign of weakness, and that a strong ruler would never have forgiven his foes.
He felt he owed Caesar nothing and was angry about it, since Caesar had given him nothing in return.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Brutus believed a Roman's first duty was to the city and its laws, not to any person. He thought that being spared by Caesar proved the problem.

questions.text: What did the assassins fail to do?

answers.text: They failed to choose a day when the Senate was meeting.
They failed to ask Caesar's soldiers to join them beforehand, and so the army stayed loyal to Caesar.
They thought only about the killing and made no plan for Antony, the army, or the city.
They failed to name Brutus dictator at once, and so there was no leader when the Senate hall emptied.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the assassins thought only about the knife and almost nothing about the morning after. They had no army and no plan to win over Caesar's soldiers, and they hoped the Republic would simply return.

questions.text: Why did the crowd turn against the assassins after Caesar's death?

answers.text: Brutus's speech was too long, and the crowd grew tired and began to drift away from the Forum.
The Senate declared that Caesar was a god, and the people could no longer speak against him in public.
Cassius spoke against Caesar's will, and the crowd was angry that anyone should dispute the dead man.
Antony read out Caesar's will, which left money to every citizen, and showed the crowd the bloody robe.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Antony, a gifted speaker, read out the will and showed the robe. The crowd grew furious and burned the body in the Forum, and Brutus and Cassius had to flee.

quizzes.title: 34.1 Reading Quiz: Octavian, Antony, and the Second Triumvirate

questions.text: Octavian was young, often sick, and no great soldier, yet within months he had an army. What explains this?

answers.text: The Senate gave him command of its legions, because it hoped that he would turn them against Antony.
Caesar's veterans heard the name of their old general and rallied to his son.
He paid his soldiers out of his own treasure, which he had taken from the lands that Caesar left him.
