questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar's name was worth more than gold, and soldiers who had served under Caesar would follow his son almost anywhere.

questions.text: Cicero hoped to use Octavian against Antony and then push him aside. Why did that plan fail?

answers.text: Octavian refused to meet with anyone, so Cicero could not speak to him.
Cicero was killed before he could speak again, and so the plan came to an end before it had begun.
Antony beat Octavian in the first battle, and Octavian was forced to run away from the city.
Octavian made peace with Antony, because each man had something the others needed.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that in 43 BC Octavian made peace with Antony. Antony had experience and an army, Lepidus had troops near Rome, and Octavian had the name of Caesar.

questions.text: The lesson says the Second Triumvirate was different from the first. What was the difference?

answers.text: It was made legal by a vote, so each man held great power and no one could check him.
It was a private deal with no real power, so the Senate still ruled.
It included Cicero as a fourth member, and he spoke for the Senate in the meetings of the three men.
It was meant to last for the lifetime of its members, and no vote could ever bring it to an end.

questions.feedback_general: The first triumvirate, with Pompey, Caesar, and Crassus, was a private deal. This one was made legal by a vote, and it was to last five years.

questions.text: Why did the three men publish the lists called proscriptions?

answers.text: To make a record of Romans who had died in the wars.
To give the Senate more power over the army, since the lists named the officers who were to be removed.
To pay their armies from the dead men's property and to take revenge on their enemies.
To protect Rome from enemies outside Italy, since the men on the lists had plotted with foreign kings.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says they wanted money for their armies and revenge on their enemies. The killer was paid, and the state took the dead man's property to buy loyalty.

questions.text: Appian tells of slaves who betrayed their masters, and also of wives and slaves who risked their lives to save people on the lists. What can we infer?

answers.text: All Romans behaved cruelly during the proscriptions, and no one showed any pity for the people on the lists.
The terror pushed some people to betray and others to risk everything for those they loved.
Nobody dared to help anyone on the lists, since the soldiers were in every street and house of the city.
Appian made up the loyal ones to improve his story.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson reports both kinds of stories. Fear and reward brought out the worst in some people and the best in others.

quizzes.title: 34.2 Reading Quiz: Actium and the First Emperor

questions.text: Octavian declared war on Cleopatra, not on Antony. Why was that clever?

answers.text: It let him avoid fighting at sea, where Antony's fleet was strong.
It made Antony his ally, since Antony would then agree to fight against the queen on Rome's side.
It made the war look like a fight against a foreign enemy and not another civil war.
It forced the Senate to give up its power, since only Octavian could lead the war against the queen.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that this made it look like a war against a foreign enemy, and that it worked. After years of civil war, Romans were tired of Romans killing Romans.

questions.text: Octavian made Egypt his own property, and no senator could enter without his leave. What does this suggest?

answers.text: Egypt was too poor to matter, and Octavian only wanted to keep the senators away from its quarrels.
Senators did not like to travel, and so Octavian kept them at home in order to spare them the trip.
Egypt had no grain, and so the country was of no use to anyone except the priests of its temples.
Egypt's grain fed Rome, so whoever held Egypt held the key to the city's food, and he wanted no rival there.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the grain of the Nile would feed Rome, and that he would hold the key. Keeping senators out kept any rival from using Egypt against him.

questions.text: In 27 BC the Senate looked after the peaceful lands and Augustus held the provinces where most of the army was stationed. What does this show?

answers.text: Real power stayed with the man who held the army, whatever the old names said.
Real power had moved back to the Senate, which chose the governors.
The people now held the real power, since the assemblies voted on every law that Augustus proposed.
Augustus had no army left, since he had sent his soldiers home and given them all farms to work.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls this the heart of the matter. The Republic's offices and names stayed, but the man with the legions held the power.

questions.text: Augustus wrote a long list of his deeds called the Res Gestae. Why should a careful reader not rely on it alone?

answers.text: It was written in a language that nobody could read, and scholars had to guess at what it said.
A man who lists his own deeds chooses what to include, and this one leaves out the proscriptions.
It was written by his enemies, who wanted to make Augustus look foolish in the eyes of the Romans.
It says nothing about temples or games, and so it leaves out the things that Augustus cared about most.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he is not lying about the temples or the games, but a list of one's own deeds is not a neutral report. We should ask what he leaves out and what he wants readers to think.

questions.text: The lesson says few people noticed the change from Republic to rule by one man, and that was what Augustus wanted. Why would he want that?

answers.text: Romans loved kings and wanted one, and Augustus did not want to disappoint them by refusing the crown.
The Senate had begged to be ruled, and Augustus agreed quietly.
He wanted to be remembered as harsh, and so he made the change slowly to give his enemies time to fear him.
Romans hated the idea of a king, and Caesar had been killed for looking like one.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Augustus had seen what happened to Caesar. By keeping the old offices, names, and costumes, he held a king's power without a king's title.

quizzes.title: 35.1 Reading Quiz: The Pax Romana: Governing an Empire

questions.text: Rome let city councils in Gaul and Greece run their own streets and festivals, as long as taxes were paid and order was kept. Why was this a secret of Rome's success?

answers.text: Rome did not care what happened in the provinces, so towns did as they liked.
It needed fewer officials and gave people less reason to rebel, so peace was cheaper to keep.
It made all provinces equal to Rome, and every free man in the empire could vote in the city's assemblies.
It let each town raise its own army, and so the provinces could defend themselves from any raid or revolt.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls this light touch a secret of Rome's success. Local people kept running their own towns, so Rome did not have to govern every street.

questions.text: The legions were stationed at the borders and not in the cities. What does this suggest about how Rome kept the peace?

answers.text: Its army was aimed mainly at enemies outside, so most provinces saw few soldiers.
Rome did not trust its soldiers, so it kept them far from the cities.
Rome had no need of an army, since the roads and the laws were enough to keep the peace in the provinces.
The cities had their own armies, which kept order inside the walls while the legions watched the roads.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the empire had about thirty legions stationed at its borders. Inside, the roads, the courts, and the governors kept order.

questions.text: A silver denarius looked the same in Spain and in Syria. Why did that help trade?

answers.text: Coins were free for merchants, since the emperor wanted to see goods move from one province to another.
Merchants did not have to travel, since coins carried the news home.
Only soldiers were allowed to use coins, and the merchants had to trade through the army's own officers.
A merchant could trust the coin to be worth the same anywhere, so trade moved easily.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that because a coin looked the same in Spain and Syria, trade moved easily.

questions.text: The lesson says Rome survived the Year of the Four Emperors because the system had become deeper than any one man. What does this mean?

answers.text: Emperors no longer mattered, and the Senate ran the empire without them.
Vespasian was the strongest general in Roman history, and no one dared to stand against his legions.
Roads, laws, provinces, and an army kept working even while the throne was in dispute.
The Senate took back its old power, and the Republic was restored for as long as the quarrel lasted.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says four generals fought for the throne in AD 69, but the empire held together. The ordinary work of governing went on.

questions.text: Marcus Aurelius passed the throne to his own son Commodus, who was a poor ruler. What does the lesson say this shows?

answers.text: The empire's good fortune depended on good men, and good men are never certain.
Sons always rule badly, so no emperor should pass on the throne.
The Senate should have chosen the emperor, since the senators knew the needs of the empire best.
Marcus Aurelius was a poor emperor himself, and the troubles of Commodus were only the end of a long decline.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the first four Good Emperors each chose a skilled heir. When a son simply inherited the throne, the luck ran out.

quizzes.title: 35.2 Reading Quiz: Rome's Frontiers: Germans, Jews, and Persians

questions.text: Arminius was a German chief who had served in the Roman army. How did that help him destroy three legions?

answers.text: It made the Germans trust Rome, and so they let Varus march his legions deep into the forest.
It gave him command of Varus's army, and he turned it on Rome.
It taught him Roman law, which the Germans admired and then used to govern their own villages.
He knew how the Romans fought and could lead them into a trap.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he knew how the Romans fought. He tricked Varus into marching through the dark, wet Teutoburg Forest, where the Germans fell on them from the trees.

questions.text: Tacitus gives the chief Calgacus a speech saying that Romans make a desert and call it peace, but he almost certainly wrote it himself. Why might a Roman put such words in an enemy's mouth?

answers.text: Calgacus wrote them down himself, and Tacitus only copied the speech into his history for his readers.
Perhaps he wanted to show that some Romans were uneasy about their own empire, though these are not the chief's real words.
The emperor ordered him to write it, because Rome wished to show that its enemies were fierce and proud.
He wanted the Caledonians to win, and so he gave their chief the finest words that he could write.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Tacitus was the son-in-law of the Roman general there and chose to put those words in an enemy's mouth, and that this should make us think.

questions.text: Josephus says that Titus tried to save the Temple and that a soldier set it on fire by accident. Why do some scholars doubt him?

answers.text: Josephus never saw Jerusalem, and so he had to rely on the stories that were told by the soldiers.
Josephus wrote in secret and hid his name, so the book may not be his.
Josephus wrote for Rome, so he had a reason to blame Rome as little as he could.
Josephus hated Titus, and so he would have wanted to blame the general for everything that happened.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he was a Jewish commander who joined the Romans and wrote for Rome. A writer who depends on his readers may tell the story in a way that is kind to them.

questions.text: Parthia sat between Rome and Han China, and Parthian merchants kept a share of every sale on the Silk Road. What can we infer?

answers.text: Parthia gained from sitting between the two great empires, so it had reason to keep its place.
Parthia was weak and had no trade, and so it had nothing to offer to either of its neighbors.
Rome controlled the Silk Road completely, and the Parthians were only the guides on the last miles.
Han China did not trade with anyone, and so the Parthians had to carry the silk across the sea.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says silk and other goods passed from China along the Silk Road, and Parthian merchants kept a share. An empire that profits from the middle has a reason to guard it.

questions.text: During the crisis after AD 235, many cities built walls. Why was that a sign of how far things had fallen?

answers.text: The Senate had ordered it to honor the emperors, and each wall was named after the ruler of the time.
The walls were meant to help collect taxes, since every traveler had to pay a toll at the city gate.
Raiders and civil war had made the old peace unsafe, and Rome had not needed city walls for centuries.
The walls were built to keep out plague, since the sickness had come with the traders on the roads.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says farmers fled raided land and cities built walls, which Rome had not needed for centuries. The Roman Peace had ended.

quizzes.title: 36.1 Reading Quiz: Christianity in the Roman World

questions.text: Paul argued that non-Jews did not have to follow all Jewish laws to join the faith. Why did that choice matter?

answers.text: It made Christians choose a king, and the new faith was then led by one ruler from the old family.
It forced non-Jews to leave the movement, and only those who kept the whole law were allowed to stay.
It opened the faith to people of every nation, so it could become a faith for the whole empire.
It ended the use of the Jewish Scriptures, and the churches had to write their own holy books at once.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that choice opened the door to people of every nation. Christianity could now become a faith for the whole empire.

questions.text: Rome usually welcomed new gods. Why was it uneasy about Christians?

answers.text: They would not offer sacrifice to the emperor's spirit, and Romans took that as a sign of disloyalty.
They worshiped too many gods, and so the Romans feared that the old gods would turn against the city.
They refused to pay any taxes, and so the officials thought that they were enemies of the empire.
They tried to start a war against Rome, and the emperors thought they had to stop the plot in time.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Romans saw the sacrifice as a sign of loyalty, so a person who refused seemed to be a bad citizen and a danger to the community.

questions.text: Pliny found nothing worse in the Christians' meetings than hymns and promises not to steal or lie, yet he punished those who would not give way. What does this show?

answers.text: Pliny was secretly a Christian, and so he punished only those who would not hide their faith as well.
The Christians had been proven guilty of crimes, and Pliny was only carrying out the law of Rome.
Pliny hated the Christians personally, and so he looked for a reason to punish them in any way he could.
The offense was refusing to honor the emperor's image, and not any crime Pliny could find.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Pliny made them curse Christ and offer wine and incense to the emperor's image, and put to death those who refused. Their refusal, and not a crime, was the issue.

questions.text: Trajan told Pliny not to hunt Christians out, but to punish them if they were brought before him and refused to give way. What does this suggest?

answers.text: Rome wanted Christians gone at any cost, and Trajan only wished to spare the officers the trouble.
Rome did not want a full hunt, but would still punish open refusal to show loyalty.
Rome had made Christianity legal, and Trajan was telling Pliny to treat them as any other citizens.
Rome did not know that Christians existed, so Trajan asked about them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that Trajan's reply was a middle way. Governors were not to search, but a person brought before them who would not give way had to be punished.

questions.text: Why did the persecutions fail to stop the faith?

answers.text: Rome gave them up after Nero, and so the Christians were left in peace for the next two hundred years.
Few people noticed them, since the Christians met in small houses and spoke to no one outside the faith.
Christians' courage as martyrs and their care for the sick and poor, even in plagues, made a deep impression.
Christians raised armies to defend themselves, and so the emperors found that they could not stop them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says many Christians chose to die as martyrs, and that Christians cared for the sick and poor when others ran away. It adds that Christians had no armies.

quizzes.title: 36.2 Reading Quiz: Constantine and the Christian Empire

questions.text: Diocletian split the empire among four rulers. Why did he do it?

answers.text: He wanted to retire at once, and so he gave away the parts of the empire to the men he trusted most.
He saw that the empire was too big for one man and wanted a team to keep it safe.
The Senate demanded it, since the senators wished to have four rulers in place of a single emperor.
He wanted to abolish the army and send the soldiers home.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he saw that the empire was too big for one man. The four worked as a team with the shared goal of keeping the empire safe.

questions.text: Two ancient writers disagree about what happened before the battle at the Milvian Bridge. What can we safely conclude?

answers.text: Constantine did not fight at the bridge, and so the story of the victory was told only by his generals.
Both writers are certainly wrong, and the story of the battle was made up many years after it was fought.
The cross of light must be true, since both writers say soldiers saw it.
In either story, Constantine believed that the Christian God gave him the win.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says one writer tells of a dream and the other of a cross of light in the sky, but in either story Constantine believed the Christian God gave him the win.

questions.text: Constantine kept the title of chief priest of the old religion, left temples open, and was baptized only as he lay dying. What can we infer?

answers.text: He secretly hated Christians, and he was only using them to win the support of the people in the east.
He did not understand Christianity, and so he kept the old titles until a bishop could teach him.
He favored Christians without forcing the old religion out, and we cannot be sure whether faith or politics moved him most.
He was afraid of the bishops, and so he gave them gifts to keep them from turning against him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the sources do not let us be sure whether he truly believed or wanted a faith that would unite his empire, and that the answer was probably both.

questions.text: At Nicaea the emperor presided over a church council. What does this show?

answers.text: The state and the church were now bound together.
The church had become an enemy of the state.
Constantine had given up his power, and the bishops now made the laws that the empire followed.
The bishops ruled the empire, and the emperor was only the guest who sat at the head of the council.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says to notice that the emperor presided over a church council. The state and the church were now bound together.

questions.text: King Ezana of Aksum became a Christian, and his coins changed from the old symbols to the cross. What does this show?

answers.text: Aksum had been conquered by Rome, and the king had to take the faith of his new masters as a sign of peace.
The new faith was spreading beyond the empire, and a king used his coins to show his kingdom's change.
Kush forced Aksum to convert, and the king's coins show the new faith that the Kushite king required.
Aksum had never had coins before, and the new faith brought the art of minting with it from the north.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Christian faith was moving beyond the empire as well. A coin carried the king's message to everyone who used it.

quizzes.title: 36.10 Quarter 4 Exam: Rome from Republic to Christian Empire
quizzes.description: This exam covers Weeks 28 to 36. It has 36 multiple-choice questions, and each question has one best answer. Read each question slowly and think back to your lessons and primary sources. You have one attempt.

questions.text: After the last king was driven out, the Romans called their new government the res publica. What does that phrase mean?

answers.text: The strong city, meaning the state belonged to its generals.
The public thing, meaning the state belonged to all its citizens.
The sacred hill, meaning the gods owned the land of Rome.
The patricians' house, meaning the old families ruled for life.

questions.feedback_general: Res publica means "the public thing." The state was now a republic, and it belonged to all its citizens, with two consuls each serving only one year.

questions.text: What was the task of the tribunes, the officials the plebeians won in 494 BC?

answers.text: To judge court cases in the Forum.
To count the citizens and check on their conduct.
To handle the public money of Rome.
To protect any plebeian from unfair treatment by an official.

questions.feedback_general: After the plebeians marched out of the city, the two sides agreed that plebeians could choose their own officials. A tribune's task was to protect any plebeian from unfair treatment.

questions.text: In Roman custom, what was a client (cliens)?

answers.text: A person who gave a powerful patron loyalty and support in return for help.
A slave who worked in the house of a patron and ran his errands in the city.
A tribune who spoke for the patron in the assembly and protected his votes.
A Greek teacher hired by the patron to train his sons in speaking and law.

questions.feedback_general: A patron gave advice, helped in court, and sometimes gave money or food. His clients gave him loyalty, visited early in the morning, and helped him win office. These bonds crossed class lines.

questions.text: The father of a Roman family was the paterfamilias. How did the lesson describe his power?

answers.text: He had no legal power, but custom gave him a voice in the family.
He held great power by law, and he alone chose every husband for his daughters.
He held great power by law, but custom expected him to use it with care.
He held power only over his slaves and had no power over his children.

questions.feedback_general: By law the paterfamilias held great power over his wife, children, and slaves. Custom, however, expected him to use that power with care and to consult the family.

questions.text: At the end of each day's march, Roman soldiers dug a ditch and built a wall around their camp, even for one night. What does this show?

answers.text: The Romans feared the Gauls more than any other people.
Roman soldiers were mostly hired fighters who needed to be kept safe.
Roman armies valued discipline as much as weapons.
The legions fought only inside walled forts.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says discipline mattered as much as weapons. Roman officers punished cowardice harshly, and few armies took such care.

questions.text: Besides alliances, what else did Rome use to hold Italy together?

answers.text: Colonies of Roman citizens on conquered land and paved roads like the Appian Way.
Garrisons of hired soldiers placed in every allied city to watch over its leaders.
A fleet that guarded each harbor on the coast of Italy and its islands.
Heavy tribute paid in silver by every ally to the treasury in Rome each year.

questions.feedback_general: Rome planted colonies of citizens on conquered land and built roads such as the Appian Way. Together with the alliances, they held Italy in a web that was hard to break.

questions.text: How was Sicily, Rome's first province, ruled differently from Rome's allies in Italy?

answers.text: Its cities kept their own governments and sent soldiers to Rome instead of taxes.
Its people were made citizens and sent their own leaders to sit in the Senate.
It was ruled by a king who answered only to the Carthaginians in North Africa.
A Roman governor ruled it and collected taxes, and its people had no vote.

questions.feedback_general: A province was land ruled from outside. A Roman governor was sent each year to rule it and collect taxes, and the people did not vote in Rome or send leaders to the Senate.

questions.text: Which Carthaginian general held out for years in the mountains of Sicily and later turned his eyes to Spain?

answers.text: Hasdrubal
Hamilcar Barca
Maharbal
Masinissa

questions.feedback_general: Hamilcar Barca held out in Sicily with a small force and raided the Italian coast. After the war he turned to Spain, and his young son Hannibal was watching.

questions.text: Why did Spain matter so much to Carthage after the First Punic War?

answers.text: Its silver mines paid for troops, and it supplied tough soldiers.
Its wheat fields fed the whole city of Carthage during the war with Rome.
Its harbors let Carthage rebuild its fleet in secret, away from Roman eyes.
Its kings promised to pay a yearly tribute to Carthage in gold and horses.

questions.feedback_general: Spain had silver mines that paid for troops, and it supplied tough soldiers. Carthage built a new base there under Hamilcar Barca.

questions.text: How did Hannibal beat the Romans at Lake Trasimene?

answers.text: He lured them across an icy river before they had eaten, then sprang a trap.
He placed weak troops in the center and let them bend backward in a pocket.
He hid his army on the hills in fog and attacked the Romans on three sides.
He used elephants to break the Roman line at the first charge of the battle.

questions.feedback_general: At Trasimene, Hannibal hid his army on the hills beside the lake in morning fog and attacked the Romans on three sides. The river trick was the Trebia, and the bending center was Cannae.

questions.text: The word "Fabian" comes from the Roman dictator Fabius. What does it mean?

answers.text: A bold attack on an enemy's capital.
A strategy of slow, careful delay.
A peace made after a great victory.
A general who rules without limits.

questions.feedback_general: Fabius avoided a big fight, followed Hannibal at a safe distance, and cut off his supplies. His name gave us "Fabian," meaning a strategy of slow, careful delay.

questions.text: How did Scipio prepare his army for Hannibal's elephants at Zama?

answers.text: He had his men dig a deep ditch across the plain in front of the Roman line.
He sent the legions away from the field until the elephants had been driven off.
He placed the elephants in the center of his own line to answer Hannibal's.
He trained his men to open lanes so the elephants could run through harmlessly.

questions.feedback_general: Scipio trained his men to open lanes so the elephants ran through without harm. Roman cavalry then broke Hannibal's horsemen and struck his army from behind.

questions.text: What happened to the Greek city of Corinth in 146 BC?

answers.text: Rome made it the capital of the new province of Greece.
It joined Rome as an equal ally and kept its own fleet.
It was left alone after it paid a large sum of gold.
Rome's army took it, burned it, and carried off its art.

questions.feedback_general: In 146 BC, the same year Carthage fell, a league of Greek cities rose against Rome. Rome's army took Corinth, burned it, and carried off its art.

questions.text: What did the tribune Tiberius Gracchus propose in 133 BC?

answers.text: To take back extra public land held by the rich and give it to poor citizens.
To give citizenship to every Italian ally at once, so they would stop their revolt.
To forgive all debts owed by the poor farmers and end the selling of free men.
To end the power of the tribunes to veto any law that came before the people.

questions.feedback_general: Much of the public land had been taken over by the rich. Tiberius wanted to take back the extra and give it to poor citizens, which would give Rome more farmers and soldiers.

questions.text: What was the Social War?

answers.text: A war between rich and poor Romans over land.
A revolt led by the gladiator Spartacus.
A revolt by Italian allies who wanted citizenship.
A war against the Cimbri and Teutones.

questions.feedback_general: The Italian allies had fought in Rome's armies for generations but were not citizens. They rose in revolt in 91 BC, and Rome finally gave citizenship to most of the Italians.

questions.text: What were the proscriptions that Sulla posted after he made himself dictator?

answers.text: Laws that limited the dictator to six months in office and ended his emergency powers.
Lists of men declared enemies, who could be killed by anyone for a share of their goods.
Lists of public land to be given to his retired soldiers as a reward for their loyal service.
Orders sending the old senators into exile on distant islands, far from the city.

questions.feedback_general: Sulla posted lists of names of men declared enemies of the state. Anyone could kill them and keep a share of their goods, and thousands died.

questions.text: Who commanded the eight legions that trapped the rebels of Spartacus in the toe of Italy?

answers.text: Pompey
Crassus
Cicero
Caesar

questions.feedback_general: The Senate gave command to Crassus in 71 BC. He took eight legions, and in the final battle Spartacus was killed.

questions.text: How did Pompey show his skill as a commander in 67 BC?

answers.text: He ended the revolt of Spartacus in a single battle.
He captured Gaul in about three months.
He crushed the Catilinarian plot with a speech.
He swept the pirates from the sea in about three months.

questions.feedback_general: Pirates had grown so strong that they cut off Rome's grain ships. The people gave Pompey a special command, and in about three months he swept them from the sea.

questions.text: How did Vercingetorix try to keep the Romans from finding food?

answers.text: He burned villages so the Romans could not find food.
He poisoned the wells along the Roman roads.
He blocked the roads with fallen trees.
He sent the Gallic farmers into the mountains with their grain.

questions.feedback_general: Vercingetorix united many tribes. He burned villages so the Romans could not find food, and he beat Caesar once in a battle before the siege at Alesia.

questions.text: What happened to Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC?

answers.text: He won a great victory over the Parthians.
He made peace with the Parthians and came home.
Parthian horse archers destroyed his army, and he was killed.
He was captured and held for six years.

questions.feedback_general: Crassus led an army east against the Parthians. Their horse archers rode circles around the Roman foot soldiers, and at Carrhae the army was destroyed and Crassus was killed.

questions.text: Why was the little Rubicon river so important in 49 BC?

answers.text: It marked the border between Gaul and Italy, and no governor could lead an army across.
It marked the border between Rome and Carthage, and no army could cross it in time of war.
It flowed through the center of Rome, and the Senate held its meetings on its banks each spring.
It was the river where Pompey kept his fleet while the Senate prepared for war.

questions.feedback_general: A governor was not allowed to lead an army past that line. To do so was to make war on Rome, which is why Caesar's crossing was such a decision.

questions.text: Where did Caesar's steady veterans defeat Pompey's larger army in 48 BC?

answers.text: Munda
Thapsus
Actium
Pharsalus

questions.feedback_general: The armies met at Pharsalus. Pompey had far more men, but Caesar's veterans were steady, and Pompey's army broke and ran.

questions.text: What change did Caesar make to the calendar?

answers.text: He made the year 360 days long, with a great feast at the end of each year.
He made the year 365 days long, with one extra day every fourth year.
He started the year in the month of March and named the first month for himself.
He added a thirteenth month to the year every second year to keep up with the sun.

questions.feedback_general: With the help of an astronomer from Alexandria, Caesar gave the year 365 days and added one extra day every fourth year. The Julian calendar is the ancestor of ours.

questions.text: After the civil war, how did Caesar treat most of the Romans who had fought against him?

answers.text: He sent nearly all of them into exile and took their land.
He took their land and gave it to the soldiers who had fought for him.
He forgave nearly all of them, and some were given high office.
He put them on trial in the Senate and punished the leaders of the rebels.

questions.feedback_general: Caesar showed clemency. He forgave nearly all the Romans who had fought against him, and the Senate even voted to build a temple to his mercy.

questions.text: Who were the three members of the Second Triumvirate?

answers.text: Pompey, Crassus, and Caesar.
Brutus, Cassius, and Antony.
Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus.
Octavian, Cicero, and Agrippa.

questions.feedback_general: Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus met near Bologna and agreed to share power for five years. This triumvirate was made legal by a vote.

questions.text: Why did Caesar's will matter so much to the future of Rome?

answers.text: It freed all of his slaves and gave a gift of land to each of them.
It named eighteen-year-old Octavian as his adopted son and heir.
It gave his army to the Senate and ordered the legions to go home.
It named Antony as the next dictator and made Octavian his helper.

questions.feedback_general: The will named eighteen-year-old Gaius Octavius as Caesar's adopted son and heir. Octavian took Caesar's name, and Caesar's veterans rallied to him.

questions.text: Who commanded Octavian's navy at the battle of Actium?

answers.text: Lepidus
Cicero
Brutus
Agrippa

questions.feedback_general: Octavian's navy was led by his friend Agrippa, a very able admiral. His ships were smaller and faster, and he had cut off the enemy's food by sea.

questions.text: What name did the Senate give Octavian in 27 BC?

answers.text: Augustus, meaning "revered."
Imperator, meaning "king."
Dictator, meaning "ruler for life."
Africanus, meaning "of Africa."

questions.feedback_general: After he handed the state back to the Senate and the people, the senators begged him to keep some powers, and they gave him the name Augustus, meaning "revered."

questions.text: What was the Pax Romana?

answers.text: A treaty that ended the wars with Carthage and gave Sicily to Rome as a province.
The peace made between Caesar and Pompey before the war in Italy began.
A set of laws that freed the provinces from tax in return for loyalty to Rome.
A long period of peace and order inside the empire, about two hundred years.

questions.feedback_general: Pax Romana means the Roman peace. There was still fighting on the edges, but for most people in the empire life was safer than it had been in a hundred years.

questions.text: What destroyed the town of Pompeii in AD 79?

answers.text: A great fire during the reign of Nero.
An army of Parthian horse archers.
The eruption of Mount Vesuvius.
A flood of the river Tiber.

questions.feedback_general: In AD 79, Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii under ash. Diggers have found streets, shops, and even loaves of bread.

questions.text: After AD 9, why did Rome never again try to take Germany?

answers.text: Arminius destroyed three legions, and the Rhine and Danube became the frontier.
The Germans paid tribute to Augustus in gold, and so he left them alone for good.
Hadrian built a great wall across the Rhine that kept the Germans out.
The Germans joined Rome as allies and fought in its legions on the Rhine.

questions.feedback_general: In an ambush lasting several days, about fifteen thousand men were killed. Rome never tried to take Germany again, and the Rhine and the Danube became the northern frontier.

questions.text: What happened to Jerusalem in AD 70?

answers.text: The Romans left it alone after a short siege and made peace with its leaders.
Titus's army broke in after a long siege, and the Temple was burned.
Parthia captured it and held it for fifty years before Trajan took it back.
The emperor Claudius made it the capital of the eastern half of the empire.

questions.feedback_general: After a long siege and terrible hunger, Titus's army broke into Jerusalem and the great Temple was burned. The last fort of the rebels, at Masada, fell in AD 73.

questions.text: Who was Paul?

answers.text: An apostle who stayed in Jerusalem all his life and led the first church there.
A Roman governor who wrote to Trajan asking what to do with the Christians.
A Roman citizen from Tarsus who traveled widely and preached to non-Jews.
A bishop who taught that Christ was a created being, less than God the Father.

questions.feedback_general: Paul was a Jew from Tarsus and a Roman citizen. He fought the Christians at first, then became their greatest traveler, preaching to Gentiles and writing letters to the new churches.

questions.text: What happened to the Christians after the great fire of AD 64 destroyed much of Rome?

answers.text: Nero turned the people's blame for the fire on them, and many were killed.
The Senate gave them a temple to replace the buildings burned in the fire.
They were thanked for helping to put out the fire and given land in the city.
They were sent to the provinces, and the fire was soon forgotten.

questions.feedback_general: A great fire destroyed much of Rome and people blamed Nero. Tacitus says Nero turned the blame on the Christians and had many killed in cruel ways. It was the first persecution.

questions.text: What did Constantine and Licinius agree to in AD 313?

answers.text: To make Christianity the only religion of the empire and close the old temples.
To end the persecution, so everyone could follow the religion they chose.
To split the empire into four parts and share them among four rulers.
To move the capital to Byzantium and rename it for Constantine.

questions.feedback_general: Their agreement is known as the Edict of Milan. It said everyone, Christian or not, could follow the religion they chose, and property taken from Christians was returned.

questions.text: Why did Constantine call about three hundred bishops to a council at Nicaea in AD 325?

answers.text: To choose a new emperor for the western half of the empire after a civil war.
To plan the move of the capital to the Greek city of Byzantium.
To end the Great Persecution that Diocletian had begun some years before.
A quarrel over the teaching of Arius was splitting the church.

questions.feedback_general: Arius taught that Christ was a created being, and most bishops disagreed. The bishops agreed on a creed, and the emperor presided, so the state and the church were now bound together.

quizzes.title: 36.11 Optional Cumulative Review: Greece and Rome
quizzes.description: This review is optional and is not graded. It is practice for anyone who wants another look at Weeks 19 to 36, from the Greek city-states to the Christian empire. It has 40 multiple-choice questions, and the questions follow the order of the course. You may take it as many times as you like, and the correct answers are shown when you finish.

questions.text: Where did the Greek alphabet come from?

answers.text: It was copied from the Egyptian hieroglyphs that Greek traders saw on the Nile.
It was invented by Homer so that his long poems could be written down.
It came from Phoenician letters, and the Greeks added vowel signs.
It came from the Persians, through the Ionian cities on the coast of Asia Minor.

questions.feedback_general: Around 800 BC the Greeks borrowed Phoenician letters. They changed some to stand for vowel sounds, which the Phoenician letters did not show.

questions.text: Sparta used heavy iron bars as money. Why did that suit the Spartans?

answers.text: They were too bulky to carry far, which discouraged trade with other cities.
The bars could be melted down to make shields for the hoplites of the army.
The helots were paid in bars for the grain that they grew in the fields.
The bars were sent each year as gifts to the oracle at Delphi for its advice.

questions.feedback_general: Iron bars were too bulky to carry far, so they discouraged trade. This kept outside ideas and luxuries from creeping into Sparta.

questions.text: Greek hoplites and early Roman soldiers were both citizens who owned land. How did that shape the way they fought?

answers.text: They were paid more than hired soldiers, so they were more loyal in battle.
They served all year long and never went home, so they became expert fighters.
The law punished any man who retreated with death, so they stood firm in the line.
They fought for their own farms and homes, so they had every reason to win.

questions.feedback_general: A farmer who lost a battle might lose his home. That gave citizen-soldiers, Greek and Roman alike, every reason to win.

questions.text: How did Peisistratus win a bodyguard that he later used to seize the Acropolis?

answers.text: He bribed the archons with silver from the Laurion mines to name him guard captain.
He wounded himself and his mules and claimed his enemies had attacked him.
He won a vote in the Assembly to become the archon of the city for life.
He led a Spartan army into the city at night and took the Acropolis by surprise.

questions.feedback_general: According to Herodotus, Peisistratus wounded himself and his mules, rode into the city, and claimed his enemies had attacked him. The Athenians gave him a bodyguard.

questions.text: Isagoras asked Sparta for help, and a Spartan king arrived with a small force. How did the Athenians respond?

answers.text: The people rose up and trapped the Spartans on the Acropolis until they left.
The Athenian council opened the gates and welcomed the Spartans into the city.
The Athenian army met the Spartans at Marathon and beat them in open battle.
The people fled the city and left Isagoras to rule Athens alone.

questions.feedback_general: The council refused to obey, and the people rose up and trapped the Spartans on the Acropolis. After two days the Spartans left, and Cleisthenes returned in triumph.

questions.text: Why did the whole city of Sardis burn after the Greeks took the lower city?

answers.text: The Persian governor ordered the city burned so the Greeks could not use it.
A temple of the local goddess was struck by lightning during a summer storm.
A soldier set fire to one house, and most houses there were made of reeds.
The Ionians poured oil on the walls to drive out the Persian soldiers inside.

questions.feedback_general: According to Herodotus, a soldier set fire to one house, and because most houses were made of reeds, the whole city burned.

questions.text: After the battle at Marathon, what did the Persian fleet try next?

answers.text: It landed at Eretria and burned the city a second time before sailing home.
It sailed toward Athens, but the army marched back overnight, so it went home.
It sailed to Sparta and waited there for the Spartan army to come out.
It sailed to Persia at once to bring back a much larger army for Darius.

questions.feedback_general: The Persians hoped to find Athens undefended. The Athenian army marched back overnight and stood ready, and the Persians saw the army and sailed home.

questions.text: Why did Leonidas take Spartans who already had sons to Thermopylae?

answers.text: Fathers always fought harder than younger men.
The law of Sparta sent only fathers to war.
The sons were to take their places in the line.
So that their families would survive.

questions.feedback_general: Herodotus says Leonidas chose men who already had sons, so that their families would survive.

questions.text: How did a Greek trireme try to sink an enemy ship?

answers.text: It dropped a heavy plank with an iron spike onto the enemy's deck.
It set fire to the enemy sails with burning arrows.
It trapped the enemy ship between two rows of oars.
It smashed a bronze ram into the enemy's side.

questions.feedback_general: A trireme had a bronze ram below the water line and tried to smash into an enemy ship's side. The boarding plank belongs to the Roman raven in a later lesson.

questions.text: How did Rome treat the peoples it defeated in Italy, compared with how Athens treated the members of the Delian League?

answers.text: Rome asked allies for soldiers and let them govern themselves, while Athens took tribute and forbade leaving.
Rome took tribute in silver from its allies, while Athens asked its allies for ships and soldiers.
Rome made every ally a province under a governor, while Athens gave every allied city a vote in its Assembly.
Rome destroyed every defeated city in Italy, while Athens set each league member free after the war.

questions.feedback_general: Rome asked for troops instead of tribute, and each ally kept its own government. Athens took tribute from league members and would not let them leave.

questions.text: Who were the resident foreigners (metoikoi) of Athens?

answers.text: Citizens who had been sent away from the city for ten years by a vote of ostracism.
People who worked and traded in Athens but could not become citizens.
Hired soldiers from other cities who rowed the triremes in the fleet of Athens.
Slaves who had earned their freedom and were allowed to live inside the city.

questions.feedback_general: The metoikoi could work and trade, but they could not be citizens, even if their families had lived in Athens for generations.

questions.text: Whom did Aristophanes mock in his play The Clouds?

answers.text: The kings of Sparta and the council of elders who advised them.
The generals who had won the great battle at Marathon.
The paid teachers of argument, and a thinker named Socrates.
The priests of Apollo at Delphi and their oracle.

questions.feedback_general: The Clouds mocks the paid teachers of argument, called sophists, and also makes fun of Socrates.

questions.text: What was true of women who were born citizens in both Athens and Rome?

answers.text: They could vote on matters of religion.
They could hold office if their husbands had been consuls.
They could not vote or hold office.
They could vote, but they could not own property.

questions.feedback_general: In Athens women could not vote or hold office. In Rome women born citizens had some legal rights, but they also could not vote or hold office.

questions.text: The Peace of Nicias in 421 BC was meant to last fifty years. How did it turn out?

answers.text: It was more of a pause than an ending, since neither side trusted the other.
It ended the war for good and made Athens and Sparta allies for fifty years.
It freed the Ionian cities and ended the long quarrel with the king of Persia.
It ended the democracy of Athens and put Sparta in charge of the city.

questions.feedback_general: The two sides did not trust each other, and some of Sparta's allies would not accept it. The peace was more of a pause than an ending.

questions.text: What happened to the Athenian expedition in Sicily?

answers.text: It took Syracuse after a short siege and made Sicily a part of the Athenian empire.
It sailed home when Alcibiades was called back to Athens to stand trial.
The Assembly recalled the whole expedition before it had reached the island of Sicily.
The fleet was trapped in the harbor of Syracuse and destroyed, with thousands captured.

questions.feedback_general: The Athenian fleet was trapped in the harbor and destroyed in 413 BC. Thousands of men were taken prisoner and put to work in quarries, and Nicias was put to death.

questions.text: What did Plato start around 387 BC?

answers.text: A council of five hundred men chosen by lot from the ten tribes.
A school near Athens called the Academy, which lasted for centuries.
A school at Delphi that was run by the priests of the god Apollo.
A fleet of triremes that was paid for by the wealthiest citizens.

questions.feedback_general: Plato started the Academy near Athens. Aristotle joined it as a teenager and stayed about twenty years.

questions.text: What was the Sacred Band of Thebes?

answers.text: A group of priests who guarded the temple of Apollo at Delphi.
A picked unit of three hundred men that Epaminondas added to his army.
The three hundred Spartans who stood with Leonidas at Thermopylae.
A council of elders who ruled the whole region of Boeotia for Thebes.

questions.feedback_general: Epaminondas trained the Theban army hard and added a picked unit of three hundred men called the Sacred Band. It was killed almost to the last man at Chaeronea.

questions.text: Who rode in Philip's Companion cavalry?

answers.text: Hired horsemen from the Persian king.
Greek citizens drafted from Athens and Thebes.
Freed slaves who had once been helots.
The sons of Macedonian nobles.

questions.feedback_general: The Companion cavalry (hetairoi) were the sons of nobles. They rode beside the pikemen and struck the enemy at the weak spot.

questions.text: What did Alexander do at the Granicus River in 334 BC?

answers.text: He waited for night and crossed the river by a secret ford.
He asked Darius for a truce on the near bank of the river.
He charged across the river and led the attack himself.
He sent his cavalry around the river by ship to attack from behind.

questions.feedback_general: The Persian governors waited on the far bank. Alexander charged straight across and led the attack himself, and a friend saved him in the fight.

questions.text: Who built a great empire in northern India a few years after Alexander left?

answers.text: Chandragupta
Porus
Seleucus
Bessus

questions.feedback_general: A young man named Chandragupta built a great empire in northern India. His grandson Asoka had his edicts carved on rocks and pillars.

questions.text: What did the Stoics teach?

answers.text: That a person should do his duty and stay calm, whatever happens.
That a quiet life, free of fear, is the best kind of life.
That the strong should rule the weak and take what they can.
That the stars decide the fate of kings and of whole nations.

questions.feedback_general: The Stoics taught duty and calm. The Epicureans taught that a quiet life, free of fear, is best.

questions.text: Where were the Twelve Tables set up so that everyone could read them?

answers.text: On the walls of the Senate house.
Inside the temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline hill.
In the Forum, the open square at the heart of Rome.
At the gates of every town in Italy.

questions.feedback_general: About 450 BC the Romans carved their laws on bronze or wooden tablets and set them up in the Forum.

questions.text: Both Sparta and the Roman Republic had two top leaders at the same time. What was the purpose?

answers.text: One could lead the army while the other farmed.
One could speak for the patricians and the other for the plebeians.
A spare ruler was ready if one died in war.
It helped keep any one person from holding all the power.

questions.feedback_general: Sparta had two kings, and Rome had two consuls who could each stop the other. Both systems were built so that no one person could grab all the power.

questions.text: Which Roman officials counted the citizens and checked on their conduct?

answers.text: Praetors
Censors
Quaestors
Tribunes

questions.feedback_general: Censors counted the citizens and checked on their conduct. Praetors served as judges, and quaestors handled public money.

questions.text: What was Cincinnatus doing when the Senate chose him as dictator, and what did he do afterward?

answers.text: He was leading the legions, and afterward he kept his power for life.
He was serving as consul, and afterward he made himself king of Rome.
He was judging a case in the Forum, and afterward he joined the Senate.
He was plowing his farm, and afterward he gave up power and went home.

questions.feedback_general: Cincinnatus rescued the trapped army in about two weeks and then went back to his farm. The Romans loved the story because it showed a citizen who served the state and did not cling to power.

questions.text: What did Carthage have to do after it lost at the Aegates Islands in 241 BC?

answers.text: Give up Sicily and pay a large sum over many years.
Give up its whole fleet and burn its harbors in North Africa.
Hand Hamilcar Barca over to Rome to answer for the war.
Join the Roman alliance as an equal partner with its own army.

questions.feedback_general: Carthage gave up Sicily and agreed to pay a large sum over many years. Sicily became Rome's first province.

questions.text: The fall of which Spanish city in 219 BC led to the Second Punic War?

answers.text: Carthage
Saguntum
Messana
Capua

questions.feedback_general: Hannibal besieged Saguntum, a city Rome had made friends with. It fell after about eight months, and Rome demanded that Carthage hand Hannibal over.

questions.text: What did both Solon and Tiberius Gracchus try to do?

answers.text: Take power away from the Senate and give it to a single king.
Win glory for their cities in wars fought on foreign shores.
Help poor farmers who were losing their land or their freedom.
End the keeping of slaves in their cities and free every slave.

questions.feedback_general: Solon canceled the debts that were crushing poor farmers. Tiberius Gracchus wanted to give public land to poor citizens. Both tried to ease the same kind of trouble.

questions.text: Egypt was ruled by the family of Ptolemy after Alexander. What happened to Egypt after Actium?

answers.text: It was divided among Antony's generals, who ruled it in turn.
It became a free ally of Rome with an army and a fleet of its own.
It became a Roman province held by Octavian, and its grain fed Rome.
It was given back to the priests of its old temples to rule as before.

questions.feedback_general: After Antony and Cleopatra died, Egypt became a Roman province and Octavian's own property. The grain of the Nile would feed Rome, and he held the key.

questions.text: What did Rome make of the land of Carthage after 146 BC?

answers.text: A free city under the care of Scipio.
A province called Africa.
A colony for retired soldiers.
A kingdom ruled by Masinissa.

questions.feedback_general: After the city was burned, the land became a Roman province called Africa.

questions.text: Which two tribes swept down from the north and destroyed several Roman armies before Marius beat them?

answers.text: The Cimbri and the Teutones.
The Samnites and the Latins.
The Gauls and the Helvetians.
The Parthians and the Persians.

questions.feedback_general: The Cimbri and the Teutones frightened Rome, and the people elected Marius consul again and again. He defeated them in 102 and 101 BC.

questions.text: What did Cicero do as consul in 63 BC?

answers.text: He led the eight legions that trapped Spartacus in the toe of Italy.
He cleared the pirates from the sea and then marched into Jerusalem.
He joined Caesar and Pompey in a private pact to share the power.
He exposed Catiline's plot, and its leaders were put to death without trial.

questions.feedback_general: Cicero learned of Catiline's plot and exposed it in speeches. Some Romans said he had broken the law by executing citizens without a trial, and his enemies later drove him into exile.

questions.text: Who tried to move west through Roman land in 58 BC and was stopped by Caesar with a quick march and a hard fight?

answers.text: The Parthians, who ruled the old Persian lands.
The Helvetians, from what is now Switzerland.
The Iceni, who lived across the sea in Britain.
The Caledonians, from the far north of Britain.

questions.feedback_general: The Helvetii tried to move west through Roman land, and Caesar stopped them. It was the start of the war in Gaul.

questions.text: What happened to Pompey when he stepped ashore in Egypt?

answers.text: He was welcomed by Cleopatra and joined her army against her brother.
He was arrested and sent to Caesar alive, to stand trial.
He was killed by the advisers of the boy king Ptolemy XIII.
He sailed on to Spain and raised a new army there.

questions.feedback_general: The advisers of Ptolemy XIII did not want to be caught in a Roman quarrel, and Pompey was killed as he stepped ashore.

questions.text: What did Brutus put on a coin after Caesar's death?

answers.text: Two daggers and the words "Ides of March."
A crown and the words "Dictator for life."
A wolf with Romulus and Remus.
Caesar's face and the word "Mercy."

questions.feedback_general: Brutus later put out a coin with two daggers and the words "Ides of March" on it, to show what he had done.

questions.text: What happened to Cicero in December of 43 BC?

answers.text: He fled to Egypt and was given shelter by Cleopatra in Alexandria.
Soldiers caught him, and his head and hands were nailed up in Rome.
He was named consul and led the army of Rome against Antony.
He was sent into exile in Greece, where he wrote for many years.

questions.feedback_general: Antony wanted Cicero dead because of his speeches. His head and hands were nailed up in the Forum, a message to every Roman who dared to speak freely.

questions.text: What title did Augustus use that sounded humble?

answers.text: Rex, meaning "king."
Dictator, meaning "ruler."
Tribune, meaning "protector of the people."
Princeps, meaning "first citizen."

questions.feedback_general: Augustus called himself princeps, or "first citizen." The system is called the principate, a Republic in form and a monarchy in fact.

questions.text: What did Roman builders add to concrete so that it hardened even under water?

answers.text: Volcanic sand.
Crushed marble.
Ash from the forges of Carthage.
Sand from the banks of the Tiber.

questions.feedback_general: The Romans learned to make concrete with volcanic sand. With it they built great domes, such as the Pantheon, whose dome still stands.

questions.text: Which emperor ordered everyone in the empire to offer sacrifice in AD 250?

answers.text: Nero
Trajan
Decius
Diocletian

questions.feedback_general: In AD 250 Decius ordered everyone to offer sacrifice, and Christians who refused were punished. Diocletian's Great Persecution came later.

questions.text: What new capital did Constantine dedicate in AD 330?

answers.text: Nicaea, where he had held the great church council.
Milan, where he had ended the persecution.
Alexandria, the old capital of Egypt.
Constantinople, at the old Greek city of Byzantium.

questions.feedback_general: Constantine dedicated a new capital at Byzantium, now called Constantinople, "Constantine's city." It sat on a strait between two seas and was easy to defend.
